title: The 10 Best Martin Nievera Songs of All-Time
content:
Martin Nievara is a Filipino-American singer who doubles as a TV personality. He came from a family of entertainers. As such, his mother was unenthused about his desire to do the same because she knew the stresses his father and grandmother had experienced. Still, Nievara became an entertainer anyway. His love ballads have earned him numerous platinum certifications in the Phillippines. Thanks to that, it’s no exaggeration to say that he’s one of the most famous names to emerge from the Filipino music industry in recent decades.

Here is our opinion of the ten best Martin Nievera songs ever released:

10. “Christmas Won’t Be the Same Without You”

Filipinos are Christian for the most part. Perhaps unsurprisingly, that means they share an interest in Christmas music. “Christmas Won’t Be the Same Without You” is a surprisingly enjoyable example of the genre.

9. “On the Wings of Love”

Love has a long connection with wings. After all, the Greek Eros was famous for his wings, so much so that they’re still one of the most iconic features of modern depictions of Cupid. Of course, the connection also makes sense because being in love often makes people feel as though they’re soaring high and free. Something that can be terrifying and exhilarating in equal measure. “On the Wings of Love” does a decent job of capturing these sentiments.

8. “How Can I”

“How Can I” sees Nievera expressing a more ambivalent attitude toward love. On the one hand, he’s infatuated. On the other hand, he’s hesitant to take the plunge because he’s been hurt before. That tension gives this song much of its emotional power.

7. “Kahit Isang Saglit”

“Kahit Isang Saglit” is a song from Return to Forever from 1999. In it, the narrator voices his fears and uncertainties now that his significant other is out of his life. He longs for them to return so that his life will light up again. Unfortunately, the song shows no indication that will ever be the case.

6. “Forever”

Chances are good that interested individuals can guess that Nievara has teamed up with other artists from time to time. Solo love songs can be enjoyable, particularly when they’re about something that would make more sense from a single singer presenting a single perspective. Still, there are times when a duet can produce better results. For proof, consider “Forever” from the team-up of Nievara and Regina Velasquez, a somewhat younger Filipino artist who has also established herself as a legend in that country’s entertainment industries. The pair released this song in 2000, meaning their overwhelming experience enabled it to soar.

5. “Paradise”

“Paradise” is ironically named. After all, its narrator isn’t describing a relationship in its happiest stage. Instead, he’s talking about him overcoming his heartbreak following a breakup. It’s easy to read a note of vindictiveness to the whole thing. The narrator talks about how he hopes his ex won’t feel poorly about him recovering from the breakup. Funny enough, that undermines his claim that he is getting over the whole thing. Love and hate are often held up as mirror opposites. His line of thought suggests he’s still emotionally invested in the relationship. Otherwise, he would be indifferent rather than trying to score points in the breakup.

4. “I Dreamed a Dream”

Many people see their dreams dashed to pieces. Sometimes, this is because they have unrealistic expectations. Other times, this is because they fail to put in the necessary work. Whatever the reason, many people can understand losing their dreams, whether slowly or suddenly. As such, it’s easy to sympathize with the narrator of this song, who uses rich imagery to illustrate how reality has hollowed him out.

3. “Ikaw Ang Lahat Sa Akin”

There’s something admirable about the constancy of feeling. The world might change around people. However, people can hold on to their emotions. This song is a fine choice for listeners who want to indulge in such sentiments.

2. “Till the End”

Of course, constancy of feeling isn’t necessarily a good thing. Relationships fail constantly, even when both sides do their best to keep things going. Ideally, a person would be able to move on from their ex, thus enabling them to find happiness elsewhere. The narrator of this song does not fit that mold. He has decided that the person he’s singing about is the only one for him. This work is named thus because he means to cling to this position for his entire lifetime. Unfortunately, the narrator didn’t realize this until his relationship ended, meaning he’s now trapped in a miserable situation. Theoretically, he might still move on once he has had time to cool off. Sadly, there’s no guarantee that this will be the case. Regardless, Nievara managed to sell the desired emotions effectively and efficiently in this song.

1. “Say That You Love Me”

Nievara released “Say That You Love Me” on Dream in 1989. Looking back, that can be considered the early part of his career. However, it’s worth remembering that he was already a veteran in those days, seeing as how he had already released five studio albums by that point. As such, “Say That You Love Me” was the work of someone who had already honed his craft, meaning it’s far from the awkward stumbling of an inexperienced artist. That has contributed to it being one of Nievara’s most memorable love ballads, which is no small accomplishment considering the sheer number he has recorded and released over the years.

title: U2’s The Edge breaks his silence on sequel to ‘Elf’
content:
U2‘s The Edge has spoken out after an unlikely story emerged that he had written a sequel to Will Ferrell‘s Christmas comedy Elf.

  • READ MORE: U2: “You have to up your game when people step into the room like Fontaines D.C.”

Earlier this month, comedian and actor Andy Richter revealed that the guitarist had written an unproduced follow-up to the 2003 film, directed by Jon Favreau.

Richter, who appeared in Elf as children’s author Morris, explained that the film’s producer Shauna Robertson had been contacted about the U2 guitarist’s proposed sequel, but the project ultimately went nowhere.

Now, The Edge has addressed the story himself in a new interview with CBS Sunday Morning.

“It’s an outrage for someone to suggest that I would write a script,” he joked. “I wrote a treatment – it’s a different thing – for my own amusement, yes.”

He explained that coming up with film ideas was something he had experienced several times in the past.

“This happened to me about three or four times. I will wake up, and I will have a complete movie outline in my head,” he said.

Recalling his idea for Elf 2, he added: “This morning, I woke up with this idea in my head for a sequel to Elf.”

The guitarist said he was a huge fan of the original film and had written down his ideas before discussing them with a friend who worked as a film producer.

“I think I just shared it with a couple of people,” he explained. “Honestly, I thought it was so far-fetched that I didn’t take it terribly seriously. But you never know.”

The revelation appeared to come as news to the rest of U2, with Bono asking where the story had come from and declaring: “This is very big news.”

When the frontman wondered whether Ferrell was only now learning about the proposed sequel, The Edge laughed: “He might be finding out about it right now.”

Meanwhile, U2 released their 16th studio album ‘Carnaval De Luz’ yesterday (November 13), marking their first full-length record of new material since 2017’s ‘Songs Of Experience’.

The album received a three-star review from NME, which praised the band’s renewed energy and concluded that “for the first time in a long time, U2 sound more playful than preachy”.

The Edge also recently spoke to NME about the album, describing its themes of optimism and togetherness as a response to an increasingly divided world.

“The big enemy right now is despondency,” he said. “Defiant joy is the sense that the future is something we can co-author, and not to give in to this doom-mongering.”

U2 are preparing for their ‘The Greatest Show On Earth’ world stadium tour in 2027, which will visit Latin America and Europe. Wolf Alice will support the UK and European dates, including four concerts at London’s Tottenham Hotspur Stadium in June. Tickets are on sale now – find yours here.

title: Joseph Capriati Brings “Saudade” to Saved Records
content:
Saved Records has a new name on its roster. Joseph Capriati makes his debut on Nic Fanciulli‘s label with “Saudade,” a house and techno cut the label calls timeless and groove-driven, built for peak-time floors.

The track has already had a life before release. Capriati road-tested it across his summer sets, which means it arrives with a reputation rather than a marketing push behind it. People who caught him play it already know how it lands. Everyone else gets to find out now. The label notes that it works directly with Capriati’s management on the release, a small detail that suggests a working relationship rather than a one-off licensing deal.

The title does a lot of work. “Saudade” is Portuguese, and English has never managed a tidy equivalent. It sits somewhere between longing, nostalgia, and the ache of missing something that might not return. Translators argue about it. Fado singers built a tradition on it. Naming a peak-time record after that feeling is a curious choice, and it hints that Capriati is after something with a little emotional weight under the kick drum.

That fits the description. “Groove-driven” is the phrase the label uses, and it points at a record that moves through the low end rather than leaning on a big melodic hook. Tracks in that mode tend to age well. They don’t depend on a drop or a sample that dates them. They depend on rhythm, and rhythm is the part of dance music that lasts.

The release marks a new chapter in Capriati‘s discography and a new name for Saved. It’s early days, but the fit looks right. A track with a title about longing, made for the loudest part of the night, released by a label that understands both. Sometimes the pieces line up.

title: Robyn says Eurovision is “just shit” now: “It really is embarrassing”
content:
Robyn has delivered a scathing assessment of the Eurovision Song Contest, describing the competition as “just shit” and “embarrassing”.

  • READ MORE: The Big Read – Robyn: “I danced a lot on my own”

The Swedish singer made the comments during an appearance on Amy Poehler‘s Good Hang podcast, which was released on Tuesday (November 10).

Towards the end of their conversation, Poehler asked Robyn about the importance of Eurovision to European audiences, prompting the singer to laugh before giving her unfiltered opinion.

“We don’t have ABBA anymore, so I don’t really watch Eurovision,” she began. “They were one of the first people to win the whole thing for us, with ‘Waterloo’. Hard to beat.

“Then we had Carola; both me and Zara [Larsson] grew up listening to her. Amazing artist. Now, it’s just shit, I would say.”

Robyn continued: “I have American friends that I watch it with. My friend Bart has a blanket that he pulls up over his eyes while we’re watching ’cause it’s so embarrassing, and it really is embarrassing.

“And after I watched it, I feel really just overstimulated, and in a bad way. I was looking for words I’m not gonna say. But yeah, I don’t like it.”

Sweden has a particularly successful history at Eurovision, having won the contest seven times. ABBA’s victory with ‘Waterloo’ in 1974 helped launch their international career, while Carola Häggkvist claimed the trophy in 1991 with ‘Fångad av en stormvind’.

More recently, Loreen won the competition in 2012 with ‘Euphoria’ and again in 2023 with ‘Tattoo’, becoming only the second performer to win Eurovision twice.

Robyn’s remarks come amid continued controversy surrounding Eurovision and Israel’s participation in the competition.

In January 2024, she was among more than 1,000 Swedish artists who signed an open letter calling for Israel to be excluded from that year’s contest in Malmö, alongside Fever Ray, First Aid Kit and Viagra Boys.

The letter argued that allowing Israel to participate amid the war in Gaza undermined the competition’s values. Organisers ultimately rejected calls to exclude the country.

Israel’s continued participation has since prompted further protests and boycotts, with Ireland and the Netherlands announcing that they will not participate in the 2027 competition.

Meanwhile, Robyn released her ninth studio album ‘Sexistential’ in March, marking her first full-length record since 2018’s ‘Honey’.

The album received a five-star review from NME, which described it as “a joyride that’s both serious and silly”, adding: “Post-‘Honey’, Robyn is looser, more limber; this is an album about feeling everything all at once.”

She subsequently embarked on her biggest headline tour to date, including a show at London’s O2 Arena in July that earned another five-star review from NME.

Robyn also recently teamed up with Zara Larsson for a new version of ‘Talk To Me’, titled ‘Talk To Me, Zara’.

title: Noel Fielding breaks silence on Russell Brand after rape and sexual assault conviction
content:
Noel Fielding has spoken out about Russell Brand following his conviction for rape and sexual assault, distancing himself from their past relationship and expressing regret over their jokes.

Brand was sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison on Monday (November 9), having been found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault against four women. He was acquitted of two other rape charges and one count of attempted indecent assault.

Fielding, who worked alongside Brand on numerous television, radio and live comedy shows during the 2000s, has now addressed their relationship in a statement to The Sun.

“I was horrified and deeply disturbed to learn of Russell Brand’s crimes, which I was completely unaware of until they became public knowledge. My thoughts are with the women whose courage brought him to justice,” he said.

“I appeared on TV, radio and live charity shows with him, and whilst we played it up for the cameras and in the media, I considered it a professional relationship, rather than a personal one. I have had no contact with him for many years.

“Looking back at some of the jokes I made alongside him I was appalled. They were horrible and inappropriate, and I very much regret them.”

Fielding and Brand became familiar collaborators during the 2000s, appearing together on The Big Fat Quiz Of The Year, Brand’s BBC radio programmes and live comedy events.

They also performed together under the name The Goth Detectives, including at a Teenage Cancer Trust charity show at London’s Royal Albert Hall in 2013, which was organised by Noel Gallagher.

One of their most controversial appearances came during a 2007 episode of The Big Fat Quiz Of The Year, when fellow panellist Jonathan Ross joked about moving Lily Allen away from Fielding and Brand because of their reputations with women.

Fielding responded: “How dare you – we’re not rapists,” before the comedians exchanged further jokes about sexual assault.

The footage resurfaced following the initial allegations against Brand in 2023, prompting Allen to reflect on the incident in an interview with Grazia.

She said she had laughed along with the jokes at the time, but described them in retrospect as “really horrendous”, adding: “It makes me uncomfortable, but I don’t think I felt that at the time, because it was the culture.”

Fielding and Brand later appeared together on a 2019 edition of The Great Celebrity Bake Off For Stand Up To Cancer, which was filmed in 2018. The episode was among the programmes removed from Channel 4’s streaming service in 2023 following the allegations against Brand.

Fielding has not been accused of misconduct and there is no suggestion that he knew about Brand’s crimes.

His statement follows a similar response from Jonathan Ross, who said earlier this week that he was “horrified” by Brand’s crimes and separate allegations against comedian David Walliams.

“There was a time in my life when I was on friendly terms with both men, and during that period I was genuinely unaware of their conduct,” Ross said. “My thoughts are with the many, many women who have bravely come forward.”

Ross also expressed regret over a joke he made about Walliams and a 15-year-old girl at the 2004 British Comedy Awards, saying he had not written the material and would not make such a joke today. Walliams has denied the allegations against him.

Meanwhile, following Brand’s conviction, six more women have accused him of sexual misconduct, while the Metropolitan Police are continuing to investigate two further allegations of rape.

For help, advice or more information regarding sexual harassment, assault and rape in the UK, visit the Rape Crisis charity website. In the US, visit RAINN.

title: Summer Walker’s Label LVRN Countersues For Damages
content:
The legal battle between Summer Walker and her label, LVRN has a new wrinkle. The label is now suing her for damages and breach of contract, as described in a recent filing.

According to reports, the independent label LVRN (aka Renaissance Records) filed a 14-page document in Fulton County Superior Court in Georgia against Summer Walker. It began with firmly denying her allegations of a breach of fiduciary duty, breach of contract, and fraudulent concealment, made in her August lawsuit against them.

The filing asks the court to dismiss the “No Love” singer’s complaint, and then accuses her of a breach of contract and withholding money. LVRN claimes that Summer Walker failed to pay them 15 percent of income from business opportunities they procured for her in addition to not paying them 20 percent of the royalties she received from songwriting.

“Walker has acted in bad faith and been stubbornly litigious, such that LVRN is entitled to recover its resulting attorneys’ fees,” the filing read. LVRN also alleged that the singer stopped paying an agreed upon 7 percent share of the proceeds from her 2026 Finally Over It tour, even though she had initially been paying them.

Summer Walker signed with LVRN at the age of 19 in September 2017, and signed with Interscope on an expanded joint deal two months later. The terms of the deal upon examination seemed to be “brutal”, prompting her to inform Interscope in August that she would not continue to work under those terms, looking to leave using California’s seven-year rule.

Interscope responded in October with a lawsuit against Summer Walker, claiming that her “failure to deliver” five studio albums per their contract entitled them to seek damages. The amount requested is at least $50 million, which would go to parent company UMG.

“Summer remains open to a constructive resolution. She hopes that the matter can be resolved in a manner that respects the interests of all involved, and avoids unnecessary or prolonged litigation,” said her attorney, Keith Moten of the Interscope lawsuit. “In the meantime, Summer remains focused on her music, her artistry, her children, and her fans.”

A hearing for the Interscope case in Los Angeles is set for April 15, 2027.

title: Yella Beezy’s New Life Behind Bars Comes With No Privacy And One Shower A Day
content:
Yella Beezy once had the money, the cars and the women. Now, the rapper will spend the rest of his life behind bars, where even a little privacy is apparently too much to ask.

The “That’s On Me” rapper is getting a crash course in prison living after being found guilty of capital murder in the 2020 killing of fellow Dallas rapper Mo3. And according to TMZ, which obtained the facility’s handbook, Beezy’s new reality comes with some pretty strict rules.

For starters, forget conjugal visits. Beezy will either live in a cell or a dormitory, gets just one shower per day and can wear only his boxers while bathing. He’ll also have to squeeze his personal belongings into a small storage box.

Family and friends can visit in person, but they’re limited to one visit per week, lasting just two hours.

And for anyone hoping to get a little romantic with the rapper, don’t get too excited. TMZ reports that romantic partners are permitted to visit, but physical contact is limited to kissing and hand-holding while sitting on opposite sides of a table. Apparently, even prison romance comes with a seating chart.

Beezy’s shopping options will also be considerably less glamorous than his former lifestyle. Depending on his offender classification, he’ll be allowed to spend between $25 and $85 on commissary items every two weeks.

As previously reported, Beezy, whose real name is Markies Conway, was sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole after his capital murder conviction. The verdict came nearly six years after Mo3 was shot and killed in Dallas on November 11, 2020.

Whatever luxury once came with being a successful rapper, Beezy’s new accommodations make clear that those days are over.

title: FAA Issues Nationwide Ground Stop “Due To Extraordinary Circumstances” & “Safety” Concerns
content:
What is going on? First, Outlook has been down for most of the day, and now the Federal Aviation Administration has issued a nationwide ground stop.

Are we good on the technology front lately? Apparently not. And like with everything else, this is somehow Donald Trump and his administration’s fault.

Anyway, according to the FAA, the unusual step of issuing a nationwide ground stop was “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.”

In addition, the rare alert added, “all departing traffic should remain ground stopped until further notice.”

“Inbound international flights will be managed on a case by case basis,” according to the FAA.

“FAA technicians are investigating the issue,” DEI Hire Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in an online post. “We will provide immediate updates as we have them.”

Not long after the FAA’s alert, Chicago’s main airports, O’Hare International Airport and Midway International Airport, were both placed on a ground stop due to an “equipment outage,” according to NBC Chicago.

Travelers Are Already Experiencing Chaos Due To The Nationwide Ground Stoppage

NBC News shared some of the chaos travelers are experiencing:

Deveren Werne was on an American Airlines jet that was about to take off from Indianapolis to Chicago when suddenly the pilots announced that all flights were grounded.

“At first the pilot announced that there was some kind of radio issue,” Werne, 55, of Greenville, South Carolina, told NBC News in a telephone interview. “Then a little while later, the pilot said something like, ‘There is something going on that’s more serious than that.'”

Werne, a consultant who helps manufacturers and other industries adapt AI technology, said he is a frequent flyer and this was a first for him. He said there was “a mixture of emotions” from his fellow passengers on hearing the announcement.

“Then I started hearing from other friends who were on planes, including one in Chicago who was stuck on a runway,” Werne said. “Right now our plane is heading back to the terminal so at least we’re going to be able to deplane.”

At Newark Liberty International Airport, personnel in the control tower said the situation is “a whole mess right now,” according to LiveATC. “We’re running out of space” and “there’s significant gate issues” were comments also heard on the live audio feed.

“I’m as much in the dark as everyone else, I’m not getting any information from anybody,“ one controller at Newark said, according to the feed.

This Is Not The First Time A Ground Stoppage Was Issued

Nationwide ground stops are very rare, but have happened. Following the terrorist attacks on Sept. 11, the FAA ordered a nationwide ground stop.

As recently as January 2023, the FAA grounded all flights due to a failure in the Notice to Air Missions system, which notifies pilots about potential dangers.

title: Rosalía makes history with Album Of The Year award win at Latin Grammys and performs ‘Lux’ medley
content:
Rosalía has made history at the 2026 Latin Grammy Awards, winning Album Of The Year for the third time and playing a medley of songs from ‘Lux’ – watch below.

  • READ MORE: Rosalía live in London: a breathtakingly brilliant work of art

The Spanish star was among the biggest winners at the 27th annual ceremony, which took place at the MGM Grand Garden Arena in Las Vegas last night (November 12).

She claimed the night’s biggest prize for ‘Lux (Complete Works)’, becoming the first woman to win Album Of The Year three times as a lead artist, following her previous victories for ‘El Mal Querer’ in 2019 and ‘Motomami’ in 2022.

The achievement places her alongside Alejandro Sanz and Juanes, who have also won the category three times. Only Juan Luis Guerra has won it more often, with four victories.

Rosalía was visibly emotional as she accepted the award from Juanes, recalling how the Colombian musician had supported her at the beginning of her career, attending concerts in Madrid when she was performing to audiences of around 100 people.

Addressing the audience in Spanish, she reflected on the creative risks behind her three award-winning albums.

“This is the third time I’ve won this award, and — just as ‘El Mal Querer’ felt like a dream, or ‘Motomami’ was a gamble — ‘Lux’ has been, for me, a leap into the void,” she said.

“I believe it’s very important to speak your own truth and for others to be able to speak theirs; this album is my truth.”

She also thanked the people who had supported her artistic vision, as well as reflecting on those who had previously dismissed her unconventional approach to music.

Rosalía also won Song Of The Year and Best Pop Song for ‘La Perla’, her collaboration with Yahritza Y Su Esencia. She invited the group onstage during her Song Of The Year acceptance speech and thanked Mexico for its support.

Her other victories included Best Alternative Music Album for ‘Lux’ and Best Short Form Music Video for ‘Sauvignon Blanc’, while the record’s production team also won Best Engineered Album.

Earlier in the evening, Rosalía had opened the ceremony with an elaborate performance of three songs from ‘Lux’: ‘La Rumba Del Perdón’, ‘La Perla’ and ‘Dios Es Un Stalker’.

Wearing a shimmering gold gown, she performed on a stage surrounded by clouds and dancers wearing golden halos. Watch the full medley below:

Released in November 2025, ‘Lux’ is Rosalía’s fourth studio album and features songs performed in 13 languages, blending flamenco, classical music, orchestral arrangements and experimental pop.

The record earned a five-star review from NME, which hailed it as “an arresting album of astonishing scope and ambition”.

The review praised its willingness to challenge listeners, describing it as “a record that defies the playlist-driven, bite-sized, background-listening way in which we often consume music these days”.

Rosalía subsequently took the album on an extensive world tour, with her London show receiving another five-star review from NME, which described the performance as “a true masterpiece”.

The Latin Grammy triumph comes just days after she celebrated the first anniversary of ‘Lux’ by sharing a playlist of 1,000 songs that inspired the record, alongside a limited-edition vinyl box set.

Meanwhile, U2 have paid tribute to Rosalía on their new album ‘Carnaval De Luz’, released today (November 13), with a track titled ‘The Mirror Maker (Rosalía)’.

Bono has described the song as a celebration of her artistry, while Rosalía subsequently revealed that he had approached her for help with its Spanish lyrics.

title: What Exactly Is Going on With ‘Marvel 1943: Rise of Hydra’?
content:
It’s becoming a running gag regarding these Marvel video games. Unlike the movies and Disney+ series that Marvel Studios keeps pumping out, the same can’t be said for video games like Marvel 1943: Rise of Hydra.

Excitement was understandably high when the Amy Hennig-led project was first announced in 2022 during the Disney and Marvel Games Showcase at D23.

Roughly two years later, during the State of Unreal keynote, we got an epic story trailer for the game, while showcasing the power of Unreal Engine 5.

But since then, it’s been crickets about the game until this week, when rumors circulated that it was canceled; however, according to someone close to the game’s development, that is not the case, but it is still suffering from development issues.

Per Kotaku:

The news of a cancelation announcement was first spread by fan account Marvel 1943 Rise Of Hydra Countdown, and was quickly picked up in fan circles. However, before it could be confirmed or elaborated upon, executive producer Lu Gigliotti posted a message in the Skydance Slack (viewed by Kotaku) stating that he had spoken “directly” with the “executive leadership team (Dan [Prigg], Shawn [Kittelson], Andrea [Benavides], etc.) [all Skydance employees]” and that the game was not canceled. “They asked me to make sure you all hear that directly. There is no truth to these claims.” Developers were told not to let the rumor distract them, and that the studio was “monitoring the situation” and would address it “through the appropriate channels.”

Marvel 1943: Rise of Hydra’s Troubled Development

The game’s development has also been as close to hell as it could be. According to Kotaku’s reporting, Marvel 1943: Rise of Hydra was initially pitched as a Netflix game, but was changed to a console and PC game during development.

According to the report, the game, which was supposed to drop in Holiday 2025, is playable but light on gameplay, relies on one button, and lacks significant interaction.

The game is well over budget, and the game’s length and content have been significantly scaled down from its original vision.

Kotaku reports the game is “close to done,” but does that mean we are getting the once-promising game we were salivating over after seeing the first trailer? All signs point to no.

Just a few days ago, following Skydance’s problematic $110.9 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, 30 people at Paramount Games were laid off; some of those impacted were from Skydance, but there is no indication those laid off had any significant impact on the game’s development team.

Again, we shall see.

“Honestly, this is a record about all the facets of love,” he explained. “I don’t think that we could have or I could have written about that exclusively in the years previous, but we’re here now.

“I think writing about family, friends, significant others, insignificant others, the immense soul-crushing brutality of heartbreak and how love is the only conduit to some semblance of hope – there are so many facets to the mental health issue that is love.”

He also described the new era as the beginning of the band’s “third act”, characterised by a search for peace after years of embracing chaos and confrontation.

title: Blink-182’s Travis Barker quit smoking after being “diagnosed with precancer of the oesophagus”
content:
Blink-182 drummer Travis Barker has revealed that he quit smoking after being diagnosed with precancer of the oesophagus.

During a recent episode of the Big Bro With Kid Cudi podcast, the musician opened up about the time he decided to adopt a “healthier” lifestyle over 20 years ago.

  • READ MORE: Blink-182 – ‘One More Time’ review: a surprisingly touching reunion

“I was like, ‘Oh, man, I’m having a son,” he said, referring to his first son, Landon, born in 2003. “So I started running to the freeway and back. I didn’t really know what I was doing – I was just like, ‘I gotta be healthy, I gotta be a badass dad!”

Barker went on to recall his past decision to “start balancing out” some of his “bad” habits with the “good” ones. He said getting more exercise also “helped [him] stay sober” from drugs.

“My running started getting bigger and more important to me than smoking,” he continued. “[…] It’s like therapy.”

As for his decision to stop smoking weed and cigarettes altogether, Barker shared: “I only quit because I got diagnosed with precancer of the oesophagus. ‘Cause I loved blunts and I would smoke too much. So that was the only [reason].”

The drummer said he asked his doctor if he was “serious” about the diagnosis. “He’s like, ‘This is your warning shot, Trav. Don’t fuck around. You’ve got to stop smoking’. Or I would’ve never stopped.

“I thought I could be like Willie Nelson and smoke to the day I die, you know?”.

But the drummer admitted that he still “misses” smoking. Watch the full interview in the video above.

Earlier this year, Barker revealed he and Blink’s Tom DeLonge once got so high with Cypress Hill before playing a live show that they spent the entire gig itching to go home. “Smoking before shows is not my thing,” he said, describing the experience as “so awful”.

He previously explained that his 2008 plane crash made him quit prescription drugs, describing the ordeal as “my rehab”. Barker said: “Lose three of your friends and almost die? That was my wake-up call. If I wasn’t in a crash, I would have probably never quit.”

He said he used to smoke an “excessive amount of weed” and was addicted to painkillers, to the extent that he developed osteoporosis. Barker opened up about how the subsequent anxiety and depression following the accident were so great that he once “offered a friend $1milllion to kill him”.

Last month, Barker told fans that he’d undergone surgery because his “arm, hand and fingers [went] numb” after playing a live concert. “I did a nerve test Monday after my show and turns out I needed a cubital tunnel release to fix the nerve,” he wrote.

This summer saw the release of the new documentary Travis Barker: Louder Than Fear on Disney+. The project finds the musician “battling pain, grief and the thin line between survival and surrender”, per an official description.

Around the same time, Barker confirmed that Blink-182 were working on a new album – the follow-up to 2023’s ‘One More Time…’. Yesterday (November 12), the trio were announced as one of the headliners for Download 2027. They recently played a private show in Coachella Valley, California.

title: Tomorrowland unveils 2027 Winter lineup
content:
The Great Library of Tomorrow has its complete lineup. Tomorrowland Winter returns to Alpe d’Huez from March 20 to 27, 2027, and the seventh edition now has a full schedule across its day and night stages. The People of Tomorrow will gather in the French Alps for a week that mixes electronic music with winter sports, and the music runs from the resort’s sun terraces in the afternoon to the MainStage, Cage and Planaxis after dark.

Tomorrowland Winter differs from the summer festival in one obvious way: the music happens inside the resort. Skiers and snowboarders stop between runs, boots still on, and catch a set on a terrace before heading back out.

Orbyz welcomes Charlotte de Witte, Lost Frequencies, Afrojack, Steve Aoki, Alok, John Newman, Argy, Dubvision, Ian Asher and Third Party, plus a back-to-back set from Oliver Heldens and Tchami. Frozen Lotus hosts Maceo Plex, Kevin de Vries, Kungs, Miss Monique and Mosimann, with Like Mike also on the bill. The stage’s back-to-back pairings this year are Baron with Meloko, Bhaskar with Brina Knauss, and Benwal with Olive Anguz. Life completes the daytime program with Sub Zero Project, Slander, Nico Moreno, Hannah Laing, Korolova, Koven, The Saints and Natte Visstick, and a Joris Voorn and Kölsch back-to-back.

The terraces are where the festival meets the mountain. The line between a ski break and a dance floor gets thin.

As the sun sets behind the mountains, the festival moves to the village. The MainStage lineup includes Charlotte de Witte, Lost Frequencies, Dimitri Vegas & Like Mike, Steve Aoki, Timmy Trumpet, Alok, Sara Landry, Kevin de Vries, HALŌ, Novah, Miss Monique and Ian Asher. The Cage, with its dark, raw atmosphere, has Kölsch, Slander, Quintino, Chuckie, Nico Moreno, Space 92, Hannah Laing, Korolova, Benwal and Marsolo, with Dannic going back-to-back with Dyro and Alt8 with Emilija. Planaxis brings the energy of Afrojack, Oliver Heldens, Blasterjaxx, Sub Zero Project, A-Trak, Joris Voorn, John Newman, Yves V, MORTEN, Gregor Salto and Gravagerz.

Tomorrowland Winter continues to celebrate French talent. Techno talents Nico Moreno and Space 92 bring their sound home to the Alps. Kungs, Tchami and Mosimann join them. ELFIGO, the Franco-Belgian rising star who played Frozen Lotus last year, steps up to both the MainStage and Orbyz.

Women appear across the program, from global icons to rising stars. Charlotte de Witte, Sara Landry, Miss Monique, Novah, Hannah Laing, Korolova, MATTN, Linska, Meaghan, Mila Journée, Serafina, Brina Knauss, Karakals, Lisa Korver and MANDY are spread across stages and time slots, and Brina Knauss appears in a back-to-back pairing.

The Great Library of Tomorrow gives the week its narrative frame. The festival says every performance adds a new page to the story, and the full lineup is the latest page. Alpe d’Huez is a ski resort, and the festival happens inside the resort. Between sets, people can ski, find a mountain restaurant, or stop by the Moose Bar.

With the full lineup out, planning can start. A week in the Alps in late March means choosing which run to ski and which set to catch.

title: Woo York Return to Watergate with “Levitate EP”
content:
Woo York have been making music together for almost two decades, and they still cannot say where it is heading. “I think the funny thing about being asked where Woo York is going musically is that after almost 20 years of making music together, we probably should know the answer,” says Denys Andriyanov. “But I don’t think we really do.”

What they have is the Levitate EP, a stripped-back two-tracker for Watergate Records. Andriyanov and his long-term production partner Andrew Vanzhula have spent those two decades exploring the constraints of sound and the tools that bring their ideas to life, and this release finds them back at the deeper, techno-leaning end of their range: hypnotic loops, careful detail, and the 303 basslines that have long been part of their signature. It signals a commitment to curiosity and experimentation.

“Warlock” is the more single-minded of the two. Built around the 303, it lets a sequence run for a long time while the changes happen at the edges, almost under the listener’s notice.

“We would probably describe our approach as slow-burning acid – the duo explain. We like it when a sequence repeats for a long time and the changes are almost unnoticeable, but somehow the whole feeling of the track starts shifting. It’s not really about making the 303 scream or doing something particularly complicated.

That last point matters. The 303 has been used by thousands of artists for decades, and Woo York know it.

I mean, how much more can you possibly do with this thing? But for some reason we still find it fascinating, – they say.  – Sometimes removing something makes much more difference than adding another sound.

“Warlock” that logic is audible. Layers arrive slowly, and the tension comes from what is held back.

“Levitate” takes a different route. There is more room for melody and atmosphere, and the track moves with less pressure.

There’s much more space for melody and atmosphere, which is something we’ve always been interested in too. We never really understood why music has to choose between being physical and emotional. Some of my favorite records are exactly about the relationship between these two things. You can have a very repetitive, hypnotic track that still makes you feel something quite personal.

That interest in melody has run through their work for years, and it keeps the EP from reading as two versions of the same idea. “Warlock” is the club record. “Levitate” is the one that lingers after the room empties.

The return to Watergate has history behind it. The Berlin club and label have supported Woo York‘s more experimental side, and the duo remember an earlier record for the label that used Irish bagpipes.

When I think about it now, it’s quite a strange choice for a techno record, but that’s the kind of thing we were curious about – Andriyanov says. We didn’t really think too much about whether it belonged to a particular genre. So coming back to Watergate with this release feels special. There’s quite a lot of history there, and I like that the music we’re bringing them now is different from what we made back then, but I can still hear the same curiosity behind it.

The label feels the same way.

We go way back with Woo York, both on the label and at the club – Watergate says – It’s always been a great connection, so we’re happy to have them back on Watergate Records with this new release.

Staying curious has cost them.

We’ve watched many artists from our generation completely change their musical direction as trends changed. And I’m not judging anyone for that. But we consciously chose not to. And I think we can be a little proud of it, because the decision definitely hasn’t been free.

They are producers first and live artists second. Woo York have never been a DJ duo, and their shows are an extension of the studio sessions: ideas built, tweaked, and tested in front of an audience. Those early shows found support in Berlin, the city where their sound has always sat most naturally, and the connection with Watergate has run alongside that for years.

The Levitate EP is a homecoming of sorts, then, both in sound and in the people behind it. It takes its time, and it trusts the listener to follow the details. Woo York have been at this for almost twenty years without settling into a formula, and this release shows the decision still holds.

Woo York’s Levitate EP is out now via Watergate Records.

title: The 30 Worst Karaoke Songs of All Time: Tracks to Avoid at Your Next Party
content:
Karaoke works best when the song matches the singer’s ability and the room’s energy. Some songs, despite their popularity, create problems on stage. They might demand a vocal range few people have, drag on far too long, or simply fail to connect with a crowd.

This list identifies the tracks that consistently cause the most trouble at karaoke, based on difficulty, pacing, and audience reaction. You’ll find songs that sound great on the radio but fall apart when handed to an amateur singer with a microphone. Understanding why these choices go wrong helps you make better decisions next time it’s your turn to perform.

Avoiding these songs won’t guarantee a flawless performance, but it removes some of the most common pitfalls. Knowing which tracks to skip is often just as useful as knowing which ones to choose.

1. “My Way” – Frank Sinatra

You already know this one, and that’s the problem. Everyone in the room knows how it’s supposed to sound, and your version will get compared to Sinatra’s whether you like it or not.

The song sits in a low, conversational range for most of its length, then jumps into a demanding finish. You need real vocal control to pull off that ending note, and most singers don’t have it.

If you drift flat or run out of breath during the climax, the whole room notices. There’s nowhere to hide in this arrangement.

Timing is another issue. The phrasing follows Sinatra’s natural speech patterns, so if you don’t know the recording well, you’ll rush or lag behind the music.

Choose this one only if you’ve practiced the ending specifically.

2. “Bohemian Rhapsody” – Queen

You already know this one is coming. “Bohemian Rhapsody” tops karaoke worst-of lists for a reason: it demands operatic range, rapid tempo shifts, and multiple distinct vocal characters from a single performer.

The song runs nearly six minutes, which means you’re committing to a marathon, not a quick turn at the mic. You’ll move through a ballad opening, an a cappella-style operatic section, a hard rock segment, and a slow outro, all requiring different vocal techniques.

Without a group of friends willing to split the harmonies, you’re left handling Freddie Mercury’s layered vocals alone. Most singers can’t hit the falsetto notes or sustain the operatic “Galileo” section cleanly.

Its popularity after “Wayne’s World” only increased how often it gets requested, and how often it falls flat when a solo singer takes it on.

3. “I Will Always Love You” – Whitney Houston

You already know why this one lands on the list. The song opens with a long, unaccompanied vocal run, and you have nowhere to hide while singing it.

Houston’s version demands a vocal range most people don’t have. You’ll strain to hit the low verses, then face an even steeper climb when the key change arrives before the final chorus.

The famous belted note near the end trips up almost everyone who attempts it. You either commit fully and risk cracking, or you hold back and lose the moment the song is built around.

Timing adds another layer of difficulty. Because the a cappella intro has no clear rhythm, you can easily lose track of where you are, leaving the audience unsure if the backing track has failed.

If you choose this song, expect comparison to one of the most technically skilled vocalists in pop history.

4. “All By Myself” – Eric Carmen

You’ve probably heard someone attempt this one and immediately regret it. Eric Carmen’s 1975 ballad demands a vocal range most karaoke singers simply don’t have.

The song builds slowly, then hits you with a climax that requires real power and precise pitch control. If you can’t reach those high notes, you’ll know it immediately, and so will everyone else in the room.

Timing is another issue. The dramatic pauses and tempo shifts throw off singers who haven’t rehearsed the phrasing carefully.

You might feel confident during the verses, but the chorus exposes any weakness in your breath control. This isn’t a song you can fake your way through.

If you’re set on singing it, practice the transitions between registers beforehand. Otherwise, you risk turning an emotional ballad into an uncomfortable listening experience for your audience.

5. “Alone” – Heart

You start strong, and that’s the problem. The verses sit low and quiet, easy enough to handle, so you get comfortable fast.

Then the chorus hits, and you’re suddenly reaching for notes you didn’t know existed in your range. Ann Wilson’s delivery on “Alone” is powerful precisely because she can control that jump from a near-whisper to a full-throated belt. You can’t fake that control at karaoke night.

Most attempts fall apart right at “I am alone,” where the melody climbs and demands real vocal power. You either crack, go flat, or drop out completely and let the backing track carry you.

Choose this song and you’re setting yourself up for a rough few minutes. The gap between the verses and that chorus doesn’t leave you anywhere to hide.

6. “And I Am Telling You I’m Not Going” – Jennifer Holliday

You already know this one is a trap the moment the instrumental starts. Jennifer Holliday’s original from Dreamgirls demands a vocal range and emotional intensity that most singers cannot replicate, even on their best night.

The song builds gradually, then explodes into sustained, powerful belting that requires real technique. Without that, you’re left straining, cracking, or shouting through the climax.

There’s also the breath control problem. The phrasing leaves you almost no room to recover between lines, and pacing yourself wrong means you’ll be gasping before the bridge even hits.

Choosing this song puts you in direct comparison with one of the most technically demanding Broadway performances ever recorded. Attempting it in a room full of friends rarely goes the way you imagine.

You’ll get points for ambition, but the execution gap usually turns the moment into something uncomfortable rather than triumphant.

7. “The Star-Spangled Banner” – traditional

You already know this one is a bad idea before you even grab the mic. The range spans nearly an octave and a half, jumping from low notes to a high finish that trips up even trained vocalists.

Christina Aguilera proved this point at the 2011 Super Bowl, mixing up the lyrics mid-performance despite her professional skill. If she can stumble, your odds at a crowded bar aren’t better.

The melody demands breath control most karaoke singers don’t have. You’ll either run out of air before the high notes or crack trying to hit them.

There’s also the length and awkward phrasing, both of which make it hard to keep the crowd’s attention. Choose something else, and save this one for the ballpark.

8. “Livin’ on a Prayer” – Bon Jovi

You already know the melody, but that doesn’t mean you can sing it. This 1986 anthem from Slippery When Wet demands a vocal range most people don’t have.

The verses sit low and conversational, then the chorus jumps into a register that strains your voice fast. That contrast trips up even confident singers.

The talk-box intro riff sets expectations you can’t meet without Jon Bon Jovi’s gear or his years of practice. You’ll likely just skip it or hum along awkwardly.

Then there’s the key change and sustained notes near the end. You need real breath control and stamina to land those, and most karaoke singers run out of both by that point.

It’s a fun song to shout with a crowd, but performing it solo exposes exactly where your voice falls short.

9. “Don’t Stop Believin'” – Journey

You already know how this one starts. That opening piano riff triggers a room-wide reaction before you’ve even hit play, and by the time Steve Perry’s vocal line kicks in, you’re competing with forty other voices.

Some karaoke rankings still list this as a top pick, and there’s a reason: the range is manageable, and the crowd carries the chorus for you. But that’s also the problem. You’re not really singing a song anymore. You’re narrating a group activity that everyone has done a hundred times before.

The track has become so common in bars that requesting it barely registers as a choice. If you want a moment that feels distinct, this isn’t it. You’ll get participation, sure, but not much else.

10. “Total Eclipse of the Heart” – Bonnie Tyler

Jim Steinman wrote this 1983 track for Bonnie Tyler, and you’ll find it’s built for drama, not restraint. The verses start quiet, then the chorus demands everything you’ve got.

You need serious range to pull this off. The low verses sit in a different register than the soaring chorus, and most singers struggle to bridge that gap cleanly.

Timing trips people up too. The “turnaround” lines require you to hit specific beats, and hesitation throws off the whole rhythm.

Then there’s the spoken-word bridge. You either commit fully to it or it falls flat, and there’s no comfortable middle ground.

Length is another factor working against you. At over seven minutes in its full version, you’re carrying a demanding vocal performance far longer than most karaoke tracks require.

11. “What’s Up?” – 4 Non Blondes

You know this one the moment the guitar riff starts. Released in 1993, it became a massive hit and a karaoke staple, but that popularity comes with a catch.

The verses sit in a low, conversational register you can handle easily. Then the chorus arrives, and you’re suddenly reaching for a belted high note on “what’s going on” that sits well outside most untrained ranges.

Singer Linda Perry’s original vocal has a rasp and power that’s difficult to replicate. When you try to match that intensity without her control, the result often comes out strained or shouted rather than sung.

The song also demands sustained breath support during those peak moments. You either commit fully and risk sounding rough, or you hold back and lose the energy that makes the song recognizable in the first place.

12. “Respect” – Aretha Franklin

You know this song. So does everyone else in the bar, which is exactly the problem.

Aretha’s vocal power is nearly impossible to replicate. You’ll find yourself straining for notes that require a level of control and range most singers don’t have.

The song also demands confidence and stage presence to land properly. Without her phrasing and timing, the performance falls flat, and the spelled-out chorus becomes the only recognizable part.

You’ll notice the horn section and backup vocals carry much of the original’s energy. Strip those away, and the karaoke track can feel thin compared to what you remember.

If you choose this one, focus less on hitting every note perfectly and more on delivering the attitude. That’s the part audiences actually respond to.

13. “I Believe in a Thing Called Love” – The Darkness

You know this one the second the guitar riff kicks in. Justin Hawkins’ falsetto made this song a hit, but it’s also what makes it so hard for you to sing.

The verses sit low, then suddenly you’re expected to launch into a soaring high note that most voices can’t reach without cracking. That contrast trips up even confident singers.

If you play it safe and drop down an octave, you lose the energy that makes the song work. If you try to hit it as written, you risk an embarrassing squeak in front of everyone.

There’s no comfortable middle ground here. You either commit fully to the falsetto or the performance falls flat.

Add in the theatrical rock delivery the original demands, and you have a song that rewards a very specific vocal skill set—one you probably don’t have on a random karaoke night.

14. “Take On Me” – a-ha

You know the opening synth riff instantly, but that recognition creates a problem the moment you grab the mic. The famous falsetto in the chorus sits at a range you almost certainly can’t reach without straining.

Morten Harket’s vocal delivery jumps octaves in ways that sound effortless on record but expose your limitations fast. You’ll either crack on the high notes or drop into a lower register that kills the song’s energy.

The verses move quickly, and the rhythm doesn’t leave you much room to breathe or recover if you fall behind. Timing errors become obvious because the backing track keeps its steady, driving pace regardless of what you do.

You might choose this song for nostalgia, but the gap between the original and your rendition tends to be wide. Audiences remember the iconic chorus, so a weak attempt at it stands out immediately.

15. “Since U Been Gone” – Kelly Clarkson

This song sounds simple when Kelly Clarkson sings it. When you try it, the illusion breaks fast.

The verses sit in a comfortable low range, which lulls you into a false sense of confidence. Then the chorus arrives, and you’re pushed into a belt that most amateur singers can’t sustain.

The transitions between registers are unforgiving. You either commit fully to the power notes or your voice cracks trying to reach them.

Even celebrities have struggled with this one publicly, which says something about its difficulty. It’s the kind of song that separates people who can actually sing from those who just enjoy music.

Pitch control matters here more than volume. If you go for loud without control, you’ll flatten out or strain, and the room will notice immediately.

16. “Rolling in the Deep” – Adele

You start strong, matching Adele’s low, controlled verses well enough. Then the chorus arrives, and you realize the gap between her range and yours.

The song demands power and precision at once. You need belt-worthy vocals combined with tight rhythmic phrasing, and few amateur singers have both.

Adele’s delivery relies on subtle vocal texture, the rasp and control that studio production doesn’t fully capture in a karaoke track. Without that texture, your version sounds thin by comparison.

The gospel-influenced backing vocals raise the bar too. You’re competing against a wall of sound that a single voice struggles to fill.

By the bridge, you’re either straining to hit the sustained notes or backing off and losing the song’s intensity entirely. Neither option works well in front of an audience waiting for the emotional payoff this song promises.

17. “Chandelier” – Sia

You know this one from the opening notes, but that recognition works against you at karaoke. The song sits in an awkward range for most singers, moving from a low, breathy verse into a chorus that demands real vocal power.

The “1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3 drink” hook sounds simple on the recording. When you try it yourself, you’ll notice how much control Sia uses to hit those notes without straining.

Breath support becomes your biggest challenge here. The phrases stretch longer than they appear, and running out of air mid-line breaks the momentum of the whole performance.

Pitch accuracy matters too. The melody shifts in ways that aren’t always intuitive, so you can drift flat without realizing it until the chorus exposes the mistake.

If you’re not confident in your upper range, this track will find that gap quickly.

18. “Wrecking Ball” – Miley Cyrus

You know this one the moment the opening notes hit, and you also know why it belongs on this list. The song demands huge vocal swings, from a quiet, breathy verse to a chorus that requires real belting power.

If you don’t have the range, you’ll expose it fast. The sustained notes on “wreckiiiing ball” leave nowhere to hide, and pitch problems become obvious to everyone listening.

Multiple karaoke platforms offer versions with backing vocals to help carry weaker singers through, which tells you something about the song’s difficulty. You’re also fighting against Miley Cyrus’s original delivery, which is emotionally raw and technically demanding.

Most singers end up shouting through the chorus instead of hitting the notes cleanly. Your friends will remember the attempt, but maybe not for the reasons you’d hoped.

19. “Somebody to Love” – Queen

You’ve probably tried this one after a few drinks, thinking Freddie Mercury’s vocal range is within your reach. It isn’t.

The gospel-inspired structure demands power and control across a wide range, shifting between falsetto and full chest voice without warning. You’ll find yourself straining on notes that Mercury made sound effortless.

Then there’s the guitar solo. You’re left standing there with nothing to do while the instrumental break plays out, unless you decide to sing the guitar line yourself, which rarely goes well.

The layered harmonies on the original recording don’t translate to a solo performance either. What sounds rich and full with multiple voices sounds thin and exposed with just you and a karaoke track.

Pick this song only if you have real vocal training and a genuine falsetto.

20. “Don’t Rain on My Parade” – Barbra Streisand

You need serious vocal power to attempt this one, and most karaoke singers don’t have it. The song builds from a controlled opening into a series of extended, climbing notes that demand precise breath control and range.

Streisand’s original recording sets a standard most people can’t approach. When you try to hit those sustained high notes, the gap between her performance and yours becomes obvious fast.

The tempo shifts also trip people up. You have to manage rapid lyrics in the verses, then transition into slower, held phrases without losing momentum.

There’s no instrumental break to give you breathing room either. Once you start, the song keeps escalating, leaving no space to recover if your pacing is off. For a room full of casual singers, this track exposes weaknesses quickly and rarely gets the triumphant finish it needs.

21. “Defying Gravity” – Idina Menzel and Kristin Chenoweth

You know this one from Wicked, and you probably picked it because the video looked impressive. Then the key change hits, and you remember it was written for a Broadway belter, not for you.

The range spans nearly two octaves. You’ll start comfortably, then watch the screen with dread as the final notes approach.

That sustained high note at the end is the real problem. Idina Menzel holds it with power and control. You will not have either, and the whole bar will know it within seconds.

This is a duet, technically, but Glinda’s part won’t save you. Once Elphaba takes over for the climax, you’re on your own with material built for a trained theater voice.

Choose this song only if you’ve rehearsed it. Otherwise, you’re setting yourself up for a rough finish in front of everyone.

22. “The Greatest Love Of All” – Whitney Houston

You already know this one is a bad idea before you even hit select. Whitney Houston’s vocal range is the whole point of the song, and most people simply don’t have it.

The verses sit low, then the chorus jumps up dramatically. You’ll either strain through the high notes or mumble through the low ones.

There’s also nowhere to hide. The song is slow and deliberate, which means every pitch problem stands out clearly to everyone listening.

Runs and vocal embellishments are baked into the melody. If you skip them, it sounds flat. If you attempt them, you risk missing the mark entirely.

This is a song built for a singer with exceptional control, not a casual night out with friends. Choose something with a smaller range if you want the room on your side.

23. “Unchained Melody” – The Righteous Brothers

This song asks for a vocal range and control most people don’t have on karaoke night.

The melody builds slowly, then demands a sustained high note that you either hit or you don’t. There’s no middle ground here.

You’ll notice the piano intro sets a serious tone immediately. That pressure builds throughout the song, and by the time you reach the climactic “I need your love” section, your voice has to carry real emotional weight.

Bobby Hatfield’s original vocal has a soaring, controlled quality that’s difficult to replicate without training. Most singers either hold back and sound flat, or push too hard and crack.

The slow tempo also means every pitch issue is exposed. You can’t hide behind a fast rhythm or busy instrumentation.

Choose this song only if you’re confident in your range and breath control.

24. “Careless Whisper” – George Michael

You know this one from the first saxophone note. That’s the problem. Everyone in the room knows it too, and they’re already bracing themselves.

The song sounds simple until you’re holding the microphone. The verses sit in an awkward range, low and conversational, then the chorus demands a smoother, more controlled delivery you probably haven’t practiced.

Timing trips up most singers. The phrasing is loose and soulful in the original recording, but on a karaoke track without George Michael’s instincts guiding you, it’s easy to rush the lines or fall behind the beat.

You also have that saxophone hook to contend with. It’s iconic, but it invites mockery, and someone will absolutely air-sax during your performance.

Pick this song only if you’re confident in your breath control and pacing. Otherwise, you’re setting yourself up for a rough four minutes.

25. “Rap God” – Eminem

You already know this one is a trap the moment the intro hits. Eminem raps 1,560 words in just over six minutes, at points reaching over four words per second. That earned him a Guinness World Record, but it will earn you nothing but embarrassment on stage.

Your best bet is to stick to the hook and let the verses pass you by. Even skilled rappers stumble over the rapid-fire sections, so don’t expect to keep pace after a few drinks.

The instrumental itself has drawn criticism online, with some calling it flat or uninspired. That means you won’t even have a strong beat to lean on when you lose the lyrics.

If you’re looking to impress a crowd, this song will likely do the opposite unless you’ve genuinely practiced the verses beforehand.

26. “Lose Yourself” – Eminem

You know the opening lines by heart, but that doesn’t mean you can pull them off at karaoke. The rapid-fire verses require precise timing and breath control most singers don’t have.

Once you fall behind the beat, catching up becomes nearly impossible. The song moves fast, and there’s no room to recover once you lose the rhythm.

Many karaoke versions also include clean edits or altered lyrics, which throws off anyone who learned the words from the original explicit version. You’ll stumble over unfamiliar phrasing mid-verse.

The chorus offers a brief melodic break, but it’s surrounded by dense, complex rap sections. Without strong rhythmic skills, you’ll likely mumble through most of the verses.

This track works better as a listening experience than a performance piece. Save it for the car, not the karaoke stage.

27. “Thong Song” – Sisqó

Released in 2000, this track has landed on multiple “worst songs” lists, including a St. Paul Pioneer Press reader poll that named it the worst song in history. That reputation follows it into karaoke rooms.

The lyrics fixate on a single visual detail, repeated line after line. You’ll find yourself singing about the same subject matter with little variation, which makes the performance feel awkward rather than fun.

The high-pitched ad-libs and falsetto runs are difficult to replicate without a strong vocal range. If you attempt them and miss, the gap between the original and your version becomes obvious to everyone listening.

The tempo, sitting around 121 BPM, moves quickly enough that keeping pace with the lyrics takes real concentration. You’re better off picking a song where the words match your comfort level, not just your nostalgia for the early 2000s.

28. “Baby Got Back” – Sir Mix-a-Lot

You know this song. Everyone does. That’s exactly the problem.

The lyrics come fast, and if you don’t have them memorized, you’ll fall behind almost immediately. Comedian Jo Koy has called it one of the worst karaoke choices out there, and he’s not wrong. Rapping isn’t the same as singing, and you can’t fake your way through a verse the way you might with a pop ballad.

You also have to consider your audience. This is a novelty song, so if you don’t fully commit, it falls flat. If you do commit, you risk delivering lyrics that feel awkward in a room full of strangers.

The song works best as a party gag, not a genuine karaoke performance. You’re better off picking something with a slower tempo and simpler phrasing.

29. “American Pie” – Don McLean

You know this song the moment those opening chords hit, and that’s part of the problem. At nearly nine minutes, “American Pie” turns your karaoke slot into a marathon for everyone else in the room.

You have to commit to multiple verses packed with dense, cryptic lyrics. Miss a line, and you’ll stumble trying to catch up with the next one.

The shifting tempo doesn’t help you either. You go from a slow, reflective opening to an upbeat chorus and back again, which makes it hard to hold the crowd’s energy steady.

By the time you reach the final chorus, you’ll notice people checking their phones or heading to the bar. It’s not that the song is bad—you just need a venue and audience patient enough to sit through the whole thing.

30. “Piano Man” – Billy Joel

You know this one the moment those opening accordion notes hit. Everyone in the bar starts swaying before you’ve even picked up the mic.

The problem is length. At over five minutes, you’re committing to a marathon most karaoke crowds can’t sustain.

You’ll notice the verses drag once the novelty wears off. The story about the bar patrons is charming on record, but delivering it live requires pacing and control that most singers don’t have.

Then there’s the “la-di-da” refrain. You’ll repeat it more times than feels necessary, and it starts to feel like filler rather than a hook.

The instrumental breaks don’t help either. You’re left standing there while the piano noodles along, waiting for your next line.

It’s a song you respect, not one you should reach for on a Friday night.

Why Some Songs Fail at Karaoke

A song’s failure at karaoke usually comes down to two things: the demands it places on your voice, and the way it’s structured for a live performance rather than a recording. Once you understand these factors, you can spot a problem track before you commit to singing it.

Vocal Range and Stamina

Some songs sound effortless on the original recording because the artist has years of training or studio production to help them. When you sing the same notes without that support, gaps in your range become obvious fast.

Songs with a wide range between the lowest and highest notes force you to shift registers constantly, which strains even confident singers. Tracks with sustained high notes, like power ballads, test your breath control and can leave you gasping mid-verse.

Stamina matters just as much as range. A song that stays at a high energy level for four or five minutes without a break will tire your voice, especially if you’re not used to sustained belting or rapid-fire lyrics.

Long Intros and Awkward Instrumental Breaks

Karaoke tracks often include the full instrumental sections from the original recording, and these can work against you. A song with a 30-second intro leaves you standing silently, which creates dead air and can make an audience lose interest before you even start singing.

Mid-song instrumental breaks cause a different problem. You lose momentum, and re-entering after a long pause is harder than it sounds, since you have to find your pitch and rhythm again without a lead-in.

Songs with unpredictable structure, such as extended guitar solos or unexpected tempo changes, add another layer of difficulty. You need to track the music closely instead of focusing on your performance, which increases the odds of a stumble.

How the Room Changes a Song’s Reception

The same performance can land as a triumph or a disaster depending on who’s watching and where you’re standing. Two factors shape this outcome more than any others: how well the crowd knows the song, and how the venue handles sound.

Audience Familiarity and Energy

A room full of strangers reacts differently than a birthday party packed with your friends.

If the crowd doesn’t recognize the song within the first ten seconds, you lose them. Familiarity drives participation, and participation is what makes karaoke work.

Songs with recognizable hooks or sing-along choruses tend to succeed regardless of your vocal skill, because the audience fills in gaps and forgives mistakes.

Energy matters just as much as recognition. A tired crowd late in the night won’t respond the same way to an upbeat pop anthem as a group that’s been drinking and dancing for two hours.

Consider these audience conditions:

  • High-energy, familiar crowd: Almost any song works, even flawed performances.
  • Low-energy, unfamiliar crowd: Even technically strong renditions fall flat.
  • Mixed-age groups: Songs need broad generational appeal to land.

Your song choice should match the room’s mood, not just your personal taste.

Venue Volume and Sound Quality

Sound systems vary wildly between karaoke venues, and this directly affects how your performance comes across.

A cramped bar with a single speaker and outdated microphone will make even a strong vocalist sound muffled or tinny. In contrast, a dedicated karaoke room with proper acoustics can make an average singer sound polished.

Background noise plays a role too. Loud venues with clinking glasses and side conversations require songs with clear, punchy melodies that cut through the din. Quieter listening rooms allow for more nuanced, softer songs that would otherwise get lost.

Microphone quality also affects pacing. Cheap equipment introduces lag or feedback, which throws off timing on complex or fast-paced songs. Simpler, steady-rhythm songs handle these technical shortcomings better than material with rapid tempo changes.

title: Ranking all 6 Boston Studio Albums
content:
Boston is a rock and roll band that takes its name from the city it was born in. The group formed in the middle of the 1970s and quickly became an American icon in pop culture. Their music was well-received and the group churned out one hit after another through the 1990s. This is a group that had the uncanny ability to present a set of songs that includes heavy rock to bring audiences to a frenzied crescendo, then gently bring them back down with a ballad-style song or a love song that gently moved the listener from one heightened emotion to a calmer more contemplative state. They’re among the highest-album selling bands in history with an estimated 31 million in sales in the United States market and more than double that amount worldwide. Here are the 6 Boston studio albums ranked following their popularity from worst to best.

6. “Corporate America”

“Corporate America was released in 2002. Return of Rock deems it to be the worst of all 6 studio albums released if we must assign the term “worst” to any of them. It was no surprise to discover that the album has a perfect 5-star rating on Amazon.com. This album contains some heavy guitar work including tracks “Stare Out Your Window,” “I Had a Good Time,” and the titular song “Corporate America.” The guitar leads are as always, totally up to par. It’s not my favorite Boston album, but it’s a good collection of songs with decent balance and the signature Boston guitar riffs.

5. “Life, Love & Hope”

Louder Sound ranked “Life, Love & Hope” as the fourth-best, but some others gave it a lower rating. It’s loaded with some great songs with the title song as well as “Sail Away,” “If You Were In Love,” “Someday,” “Love Got Away,” and others. Somehow this album just doesn’t pack the punch that we expect from Boston. It’s a solid project, but none of the songs are among their biggest hits of all time. The album was released in 2013, but it didn’t come close to becoming as popular as some of the others that contain their biggies including “More Than a Feeling,” and the more iconic Boston tunes.

4. “Boston”

“Boston” was released in 1976. This was the debut album for the group, self-titled, that served as an introduction to the world. It became one of the best-selling albums of the group and is now a classic for Boston fans. It’s more than that. The “Boston” album is essential. It contains some of their most popular song including “Peace of Mind,” “More Than A Feeling,” “Smokin'” and “Foreplay/Long Time.” This album defined who Boston was as a group, and it set the precedent for the songs which would follow.

3. “Walk On”

“Walk On” came out in 1994. It was the fourth album that the band released. The biggest merit of this project is that it stayed true to the form that Boston had already established. The group was in its second decade and it was still turning out lyrically sound tunes with dynamic instrumentals. It’s a balanced album that includes the pleading song “I Need Your Love,” with “Get Organ-ized” heating things up. “Livin” For You” is a well-written song that makes us all think about what it’s like to be in love for the first time. It’s not the best Boston album of all time, but it’s hard to find anything to criticize. None of my personal favorites are on this album, but that’s a matter of preference.

2. Third Stage”

“Third Stage” dropped in 1986. This is an album that was a long time in the making. Tom Scholz would settle for nothing less than perfection and it took him that long to feel satisfied that he had the quality in content and music to put it out into the world for all the Boston fans to judge. The songs are all good lyrically, as are the vocals and instrumentals. It’s a solid album with exceptional balance. It contains one of Boston’s biggest hits, “Amanda.” I would have bought it for that song alone. “Third Stage deserves the second place in our ranking, but there is an even better one.

1. “Don’t Look Back”

The best Boston album of all time is “Don’t Look Back.” The album dropped two years after the band made its debut with the “Boston” album. Their first release set the bar high, but Boston didn’t suffer the same fate as many other bands. They put together a collation of tracks that left us feeling satisfied, no pun intended, because one song on the album is titled “Feelin’ Satisfied.” “It’s Easy,” “Foreplay/Longtime” is enough to inspire you to get up out of your seats and clap your hands. Musicianship in this album is nothing short of masterful.

The precision of the rhythms and intricate guitar riffs affects the listener at deep, if not spiritual, levels. A favorite, “A Man I’ll Never Be,” is a lyrical masterpiece. Most men can relate to it at a deep level. It tempered the album with ballast for the more upbeat songs. I find “Don’t Look Back” to be one of the most balanced works by the band, and one of the finest showcases of their songwriting, singing and playing talents. They showed us who they were and what the group could do with the “Boston” self-titled album, but they took it to the next level with the content of “Don’t Look Back.” It will always be my favorite Boston album of all time.
