title: The 30 Greatest Guitarists of All Time: Ranked and Reviewed
content:
Ask ten music fans to name the greatest guitarist of all time and you might get ten different answers. Some people want speed and fireworks, while others care more about tone, feel and a riff they can hum.

This list looks at three things: technical skill, a sound you can recognize in a few notes, and influence on the players who came after. That mix brings together blues pioneers, rock gods, jazz masters and a few players who changed the instrument itself.

The list runs from the Delta blues of the 1930s to the alternative rock of the 1990s, and every name on it left recordings that guitarists still study today.

If you like this one, you might also enjoy our list of the greatest guitar solos of all time and our ranking of the greatest drummers of all time.

1. Jimi Hendrix

Jimi Hendrix is the name that tops more “greatest guitarist” lists than any other, and for good reason. Born in Seattle in 1942, he moved to London in 1966, formed the Jimi Hendrix Experience and became a star almost overnight with songs like “Purple Haze,” “Foxy Lady” and “The Wind Cries Mary.”

Hendrix turned feedback, fuzz and the wah-wah pedal into real musical tools instead of accidents. He was left-handed and played a right-handed Fender Stratocaster flipped over and restrung, and he often wrapped his thumb over the neck to play bass notes while his fingers played chords and melody.

His 1968 album Electric Ladyland is still one of the most studied guitar records in rock. His version of “The Star-Spangled Banner” at Woodstock in 1969 became one of the defining moments of the decade. He died in 1970 at just 27, and the Experience was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1992.

2. B.B. King

B.B. King could say more with one note than most guitarists say with a hundred. Born Riley B. King in Mississippi in 1925, he became the best-known blues musician in the world and toured almost nonstop for decades.

King rarely played fast runs or chords. Instead, he built his style on string bends and a quick, shaking vibrato that made the guitar sound like a human voice. He often sang a line and then answered it with a short guitar phrase, a call-and-response style that blues and rock players copied for generations.

He named his guitars Lucille, and the name became part of his legend. His 1965 album Live at the Regal is often called one of the greatest live blues records, and “The Thrill Is Gone” became his biggest hit in 1970. He was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1987.

3. Eric Clapton

Eric Clapton was so admired in mid-1960s London that fans wrote “Clapton is God” on city walls. Born in Ripley, Surrey, in 1945, he made his name with the Yardbirds and John Mayall’s Bluesbreakers before forming Cream with Jack Bruce and Ginger Baker in 1966.

Clapton took the sound of American blues players like Robert Johnson, B.B. King and Freddie King and played it louder and longer for rock audiences. With Cream, he stretched songs like “Crossroads” and “Sunshine of Your Love” into long improvised jams.

In 1970 he recorded “Layla” with Derek and the Dominos, and he later had solo hits like “Wonderful Tonight” and “Tears in Heaven.” His black Fender Stratocaster, nicknamed “Blackie,” is one of the most famous guitars in rock. Clapton is the only artist inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame three times: with the Yardbirds, with Cream and as a solo artist.

4. Jimmy Page (Led Zeppelin)

Jimmy Page was one of London’s busiest session guitarists before he joined the Yardbirds in 1966. When that band fell apart, he formed Led Zeppelin in 1968, and it became one of the biggest rock bands in the world.

Page could move from heavy riffs like “Whole Lotta Love” and “Black Dog” to the acoustic folk of “Stairway to Heaven” and the Eastern feel of “Kashmir.” He used alternate tunings, played a violin bow across the strings on “Dazed and Confused” and made the double-neck Gibson EDS-1275 famous on stage. His main guitar was a Gibson Les Paul, though he recorded the “Stairway” solo on a Fender Telecaster.

Page also produced every Led Zeppelin album. His way of layering guitars and recording drums in big rooms shaped how hard rock records sounded for decades. Few players have built as many famous riffs.

5. Chuck Berry

If rock and roll guitar has a starting point, it is Chuck Berry. Starting with “Maybellene” in 1955, he recorded a string of hits for Chess Records, including “Roll Over Beethoven,” “Sweet Little Sixteen” and “Johnny B. Goode.”

His style was built on double-stop licks (two notes played at once) and a driving rhythm borrowed from boogie-woogie piano. The opening of “Johnny B. Goode” is one of the most copied guitar intros ever, and almost every beginner rock guitarist learns it.

Berry was also a great showman, and his “duck walk” across the stage became his trademark. The Beatles covered “Roll Over Beethoven,” and the Rolling Stones’ first single was a Berry song, “Come On.” Keith Richards has called him one of his biggest heroes. In 1986, Berry was part of the first group of artists inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.

6. Robert Johnson

Robert Johnson recorded just 29 songs, yet he may be the most influential blues guitarist who ever lived. Born in Mississippi in 1911, he recorded at two sessions, in San Antonio in 1936 and Dallas in 1937, and died in 1938 at 27.

Those recordings include “Cross Road Blues,” “Sweet Home Chicago,” “Love in Vain” and “Hellhound on My Trail.” Johnson played a walking bass line with his thumb while picking melody and slide parts on the higher strings, which made one acoustic guitar sound like two players.

His records were little known until Columbia released the album King of the Delta Blues Singers in 1961. It became a bible for young British musicians. Cream turned “Cross Road Blues” into “Crossroads,” the Rolling Stones covered “Love in Vain,” and Eric Clapton later recorded a whole album of Johnson songs. The legend that he sold his soul at a crossroads only added to his fame.

7. Prince

Prince is usually remembered as a pop star, but many guitarists rank him among the best players of his era. He mixed Hendrix-style fire with funk rhythm and soul, and he often played most or all of the instruments on his own records.

“Let’s Go Crazy” ends with one of the wildest solos of the 1980s, while the long solo at the end of “Purple Rain” shows how much feeling he could put into slow, sustained notes. His most-used guitar was a Hohner Telecaster-style model, and he also played the custom “Cloud” guitars first built for the Purple Rain era.

One of his most famous guitar moments came at the 2004 Rock and Roll Hall of Fame ceremony, the year he was inducted. During an all-star tribute performance of “While My Guitar Gently Weeps,” Prince stepped forward and played a long solo that stole the show. The clip is still one of the most-watched guitar videos online.

8. Eddie Van Halen

Eddie Van Halen changed rock guitar almost overnight in 1978. On Van Halen’s debut album, the short instrumental “Eruption” showed off his two-handed tapping, a technique he did not invent but made famous. Within a few years, guitarists everywhere were trying to copy it.

He also used harmonics, dive bombs with the whammy bar and a hot, crunchy amp tone he called his “brown sound.” His homemade “Frankenstrat,” a Stratocaster-style guitar he put together from parts and painted with red, white and black stripes, became one of the most famous guitars in rock.

What set him apart was that he wrote real songs, too. “Runnin’ with the Devil,” “Panama,” “Hot for Teacher” and the keyboard-driven “Jump” were big radio hits. Van Halen joined the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2007, and Eddie died in 2020 after a long battle with cancer.

9. Sister Rosetta Tharpe

Long before rock and roll had a name, Sister Rosetta Tharpe was playing it in church. Born Rosetta Nubin in Arkansas in 1915, she began performing as a small child alongside her mother, who was a traveling evangelist.

Tharpe sang gospel songs, but she played guitar like a blues star, with sharp single-note runs and hard picking. By the 1940s she was playing electric guitar, and her 1944 recording “Strange Things Happening Every Day” crossed over to Billboard’s race records chart, which was rare for a gospel song.

She later played a white Gibson SG, and in 1951 about 25,000 fans paid to watch her wedding and concert at Griffith Stadium in Washington, D.C. Chuck Berry, Elvis Presley, Little Richard and Johnny Cash all admired her, and many historians now call her the godmother of rock and roll. She was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2018 with the Award for Early Influence.

10. David Gilmour (Pink Floyd)

David Gilmour joined Pink Floyd in 1968 and soon became the voice of the band’s guitar sound. He played on their biggest albums, including The Dark Side of the Moon, Wish You Were Here and The Wall.

Gilmour is not a fast player. He picks fewer notes, bends them slowly and lets them ring, using delay and sustain to fill the space. Fans often name his second solo on “Comfortably Numb” as one of the greatest guitar solos ever recorded, and his work on “Time,” “Money” and “Shine On You Crazy Diamond” shows the same patient style.

His black Fender Stratocaster, used on many of those records, became so famous that Fender released a copy of it. Gilmour has also released solo albums, and his tone is still the model for countless players who care more about feel than speed. Pink Floyd entered the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1996.

11. Jeff Beck

Jeff Beck replaced Eric Clapton in the Yardbirds in 1965 and briefly shared the lead guitar role with Jimmy Page. He then formed the Jeff Beck Group, which featured a young Rod Stewart on vocals and Ronnie Wood on bass.

In 1975 he released Blow by Blow, an all-instrumental album that mixed rock with jazz fusion and became a hit without a singer. Its follow-up, Wired, went even further in that direction.

Beck’s playing was full of surprises. He gave up the pick for much of his later career and shaped notes with his fingers, the whammy bar and the volume knob, making the guitar sound almost like a voice. Many famous guitarists called him the most gifted player of their generation, even though he never sold as many records as his old bandmates. He was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame twice, with the Yardbirds and as a solo artist, and died in 2023 at 78.

12. Carlos Santana

You can usually recognize Carlos Santana in a few notes. His tone is warm and singing, and his solos favor long, sustained notes over speed.

Santana’s band became famous after a powerful set at Woodstock in 1969, mixing blues rock with Latin rhythms and percussion. The 1970 album Abraxas brought two of his best-known songs, “Black Magic Woman” and “Oye Como Va.”

He played Gibson guitars early on and later became closely tied to PRS guitars, which make his signature models. In 1999, almost 30 years after Woodstock, he released Supernatural, which included the hit “Smooth” with Rob Thomas and won eight Grammy Awards in one night, tying Michael Jackson’s record at the time. Santana was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1998.

13. Keith Richards (The Rolling Stones)

Keith Richards has never cared much about flashy solos. As the Rolling Stones’ guitarist since 1962, he has built his reputation on riffs, groove and rhythm instead.

His most famous trick is open G tuning with the low string removed, which leaves five strings tuned to a chord. You can hear it on “Honky Tonk Women,” “Brown Sugar” and “Start Me Up.” He wrote the fuzz riff for “(I Can’t Get No) Satisfaction” in 1965, one of the most famous riffs in rock.

Richards plays Fender Telecasters more than any other guitar, along with Gibsons over the years. Together with Mick Jagger, he wrote most of the Stones’ songs. He showed that rhythm guitar could be the heart of a band, and that a simple riff with the right feel can last for decades.

14. Stevie Ray Vaughan

Stevie Ray Vaughan brought the blues back to rock radio in the 1980s. The Texas guitarist and his band Double Trouble released Texas Flood in 1983, the same year he played on David Bowie’s hit album Let’s Dance.

Vaughan’s sound came from Albert King, Buddy Guy and Jimi Hendrix, but his attack was all his own. He played a battered Fender Stratocaster he called “Number One,” used very heavy strings and tuned down a half step, which gave his playing a thick, biting tone.

Albums like Couldn’t Stand the Weather and In Step showed off songs like “Pride and Joy,” “Cold Shot” and his take on Hendrix’s “Voodoo Child (Slight Return).” Vaughan died in a helicopter crash in 1990 at 35. Players like John Mayer and Kenny Wayne Shepherd have named him as a major influence.

15. John McLaughlin

John McLaughlin is a guitarist’s guitarist, admired for blinding speed and his mix of jazz, rock and Indian music. The English player moved to the United States in 1969 and recorded with Miles Davis on In a Silent Way and Bitches Brew, two albums that helped create jazz fusion.

In 1971 he formed the Mahavishnu Orchestra. Its albums The Inner Mounting Flame and Birds of Fire combined jazz improvising with rock volume, odd time signatures and very fast, precise playing. He often played a double-neck guitar on stage.

In the mid-1970s he formed Shakti, an acoustic group with Indian classical musicians, showing a completely different side of his playing. Many jazz and rock guitarists who wanted to break free of standard blues licks point to McLaughlin as the player who showed them what was possible.

16. Duane Allman (The Allman Brothers Band)

Duane Allman had one of the shortest careers on this list, but one of the biggest impacts. He founded the Allman Brothers Band in 1969 with his brother Gregg, mixing blues, jazz and country into what became Southern rock.

Allman was a master of slide guitar. He played it with a glass Coricidin medicine bottle on his finger, and his slide lines sing on songs like “Statesboro Blues.” The band’s 1971 live album At Fillmore East, with long jams like “Whipping Post,” is often called one of the best live rock albums ever made.

He was also a busy session player. His most famous guest spot is on Derek and the Dominos’ “Layla,” where his slide guitar and Eric Clapton’s leads weave together. Allman died in a motorcycle accident in October 1971 at just 24.

17. Muddy Waters

Muddy Waters took the Mississippi Delta blues, moved it to Chicago and plugged it in. Born McKinley Morganfield, he moved north in 1943 and switched to electric guitar so he could be heard in loud Chicago clubs.

His slide playing, inspired by Son House and Robert Johnson, became the backbone of the Chicago blues sound. Recording for Chess Records in the 1950s, he cut classics like “Hoochie Coochie Man,” “Mannish Boy” and “Got My Mojo Working,” usually with harmonica and piano in his band.

His influence on rock is hard to overstate. The Rolling Stones named themselves after his song “Rollin’ Stone,” and British players like Eric Clapton and Keith Richards studied his records closely. Muddy Waters was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1987.

18. Ritchie Blackmore (Deep Purple)

Ritchie Blackmore co-founded Deep Purple in 1968 and later formed Rainbow, two bands that helped shape hard rock and heavy metal. His riff on “Smoke on the Water” is one of the most famous in rock and one of the first riffs many guitar students learn.

Blackmore mixed blues rock with classical music, borrowing ideas from composers like Bach for his solos. You can hear that on Deep Purple’s Machine Head, especially the fast, structured solo in “Highway Star.”

With Rainbow, he pushed that classical side further on songs like “Stargazer” and “Man on the Silver Mountain” and albums like Rising. He mainly played a Fender Stratocaster through loud Marshall amps. Yngwie Malmsteen and many other neoclassical metal players have named Blackmore as a key influence. Deep Purple joined the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2016.

19. Randy Rhoads

Randy Rhoads recorded only two studio albums with Ozzy Osbourne, but they made him a legend. Before that, he co-founded Quiet Riot in Los Angeles in the 1970s.

Rhoads had studied classical guitar, and it shows. On Blizzard of Ozz (1980) and Diary of a Madman (1981), his solos use classical scales and arpeggios instead of standard blues licks. “Crazy Train” and “Mr. Crowley” feature solos built like short pieces of music, with a clear start, middle and finish.

He played a Gibson Les Paul, a polka-dot V-shaped guitar built by Karl Sandoval, and later a custom Jackson guitar that became the Jackson Rhoads model. Rhoads died in a plane crash during a tour stop in 1982 at 25. Generations of metal guitarists still study his recordings.

20. Pete Townshend (The Who)

Pete Townshend was never about long solos. As guitarist and main songwriter for The Who, he made his mark with power chords, slashing rhythm and his famous windmill strum.

His riffs drive “My Generation,” “I Can See for Miles,” “Pinball Wizard,” “Baba O’Riley” and “Won’t Get Fooled Again.” He also wrote the rock operas Tommy and Quadrophenia, building whole albums around guitar themes.

Townshend was one of the first players to use feedback as part of the music, and he became infamous for smashing guitars on stage. He played Rickenbackers in the early days and later used Gibson SGs and Les Pauls and Fender guitars. His loud, percussive rhythm style helped inspire punk and arena rock. The Who were inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1990.

21. George Harrison (The Beatles)

George Harrison was often overshadowed by Lennon and McCartney, but his guitar parts are some of the most memorable in pop. As the Beatles’ lead guitarist, he favored short, melodic lines that served the song.

His Rickenbacker 12-string helped create the chiming sound of “A Hard Day’s Night,” and his own songs “Something” and “Here Comes the Sun” are among the band’s best. Harrison played sitar on “Norwegian Wood” in 1965 and then studied with Ravi Shankar, bringing Indian music into songs like “Within You Without You.”

After the Beatles, his slide guitar became his signature, heard on “My Sweet Lord” from the 1970 album All Things Must Pass. He played Gretsch, Rickenbacker and Fender guitars over the years. Harrison was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame with the Beatles and again as a solo artist in 2004.

22. Chet Atkins

Chet Atkins earned the nickname “Mr. Guitar.” Born near Luttrell, Tennessee, in 1924, he learned fiddle as a boy before turning to guitar.

Inspired by Merle Travis, Atkins developed his own fingerpicking style, using his thumb to play a steady bass line while his fingers picked melody and chords. It sounded like two guitars at once and inspired players from country to rock, including George Harrison.

Atkins was also a top producer and executive at RCA Records in Nashville. In the late 1950s and 1960s he helped create the smooth “Nashville Sound,” which brought country music to a wider audience. He won more than a dozen Grammy Awards and mentored players like Jerry Reed and Tommy Emmanuel. Gretsch and Gibson both made Chet Atkins signature guitars.

23. Wes Montgomery

Wes Montgomery is one of the most influential jazz guitarists ever, even though he never learned to read music. Born in Indianapolis in 1923, he taught himself by playing along with records by Charlie Christian.

Instead of a pick, he plucked the strings with the side of his thumb, which gave him a warm, round tone. He was also famous for playing melodies in octaves, the same note on two strings at once, which became his signature sound.

Albums like The Incredible Jazz Guitar of Wes Montgomery and Smokin’ at the Half Note are still considered essential jazz listening. He often recorded with his brothers Buddy and Monk. Late in his career he found pop success with albums like A Day in the Life, before he died of a heart attack in 1968 at 45.

24. Les Paul

Most people know Les Paul because of the Gibson guitar that carries his name, but he was also a great player. Born Lester Polsfuss in Wisconsin in 1915, he was a fast, clean jazz and pop guitarist who had a string of hits in the late 1940s and 1950s.

Paul was also an inventor. He built an early solid-body electric guitar he called “The Log,” and Gibson released the Les Paul model in 1952. He pioneered multitrack recording and overdubbing, which let him stack many guitar parts on one record.

With his wife, singer Mary Ford, he used those studio tricks on hits like “How High the Moon,” which reached number one in 1951. The Les Paul guitar became a favorite of Jimmy Page, Slash and many others. He was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1988 and played weekly club shows in New York into his 90s.

25. Django Reinhardt

Django Reinhardt created a whole style of music, gypsy jazz, and he did it with two working fingers on his fretting hand. Born in Belgium in 1910 to a Romani family, he was badly burned in a caravan fire in 1928 that left two fingers of his left hand badly damaged.

Rather than give up, he worked out a new technique, playing his fast solos mostly with his index and middle fingers and using the injured fingers for some chords.

In the 1930s he and violinist Stéphane Grappelli led the Quintette du Hot Club de France, a band made up only of string instruments. Songs like “Minor Swing” and “Nuages” are still standards that jazz guitarists learn today. Les Paul and many other players named Django as an early hero, and gypsy jazz festivals around the world still celebrate his music.

26. Brian May (Queen)

Brian May co-founded Queen in 1970, and his guitar is almost as recognizable as Freddie Mercury’s voice. Much of that comes from the Red Special, the guitar he built as a teenager with his father, using wood from an old fireplace.

May plays with a sixpence coin instead of a regular pick, which adds a little bite to his tone. He is famous for layering many guitar parts in the studio to create harmonies that sound like an orchestra, which you can hear on “Killer Queen” and “Bohemian Rhapsody.”

He also wrote some of Queen’s biggest songs, including “We Will Rock You,” “Fat Bottomed Girls” and “I Want It All.” His solos tend to be melodic enough to sing along to. May also earned a PhD in astrophysics in 2007, and Queen were inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2001.

27. Angus Young (AC/DC)

Angus Young is one of the most recognizable guitarists in rock, thanks to his schoolboy uniform and nonstop energy. He formed AC/DC in Australia in 1973 with his older brother Malcolm, who played rhythm guitar.

Angus keeps things simple and loud: blues-based riffs and solos played with a sharp attack on a Gibson SG through Marshall amps. You can hear it on “Highway to Hell,” “Back in Black,” “You Shook Me All Night Long” and “Thunderstruck.”

On stage he runs, spins and does his own take on Chuck Berry’s duck walk while playing. Back in Black, released in 1980, is one of the best-selling albums ever made. AC/DC were inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2003, and Angus showed that a guitarist doesn’t need complicated parts to sound huge.

28. Tony Iommi (Black Sabbath)

Tony Iommi is often called the father of heavy metal guitar. At 17, an accident at a sheet metal factory cut off the tips of two fingers on his right hand. Because he plays left-handed, that was his fretting hand.

He made his own fingertip covers from a melted plastic bottle and started using lighter strings and lower tunings to make playing less painful. Those changes helped create Black Sabbath’s dark, heavy sound.

His riffs on “Black Sabbath,” “Paranoid,” “Iron Man” and “War Pigs” became the template for metal and doom. Albums like Paranoid and Master of Reality are still the starting point for heavy riff writing. Iommi played a Gibson SG for most of his career, and Black Sabbath were inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2006.

29. Kurt Cobain (Nirvana)

Kurt Cobain never wanted to be a guitar hero, and that is part of why he changed guitar playing in the 1990s. As Nirvana’s singer and guitarist, he favored simple, heavy riffs and raw noise over technical skill.

Songs like “Smells Like Teen Spirit,” “Come as You Are” and “Heart-Shaped Box” use a quiet verse and a loud, distorted chorus, a pattern that defined grunge on the albums Nevermind and In Utero.

Cobain was left-handed and played cheap Fender Mustangs and Jaguars, along with right-handed guitars restrung for left-handed playing. He cared about mood and tone, not solos. After Nevermind, a generation of alternative and indie bands picked up guitars and followed his example. Cobain died in 1994 at 27, and Nirvana were inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2014.

30. Tom Morello (Rage Against the Machine)

Tom Morello made the guitar sound like things it was never supposed to sound like. In Rage Against the Machine, he used a toggle switch as a kill switch, a DigiTech Whammy pedal and other tricks to imitate DJ scratching, sirens and electronic noise.

You can hear his style on “Killing in the Name” and “Bulls on Parade,” where crushing riffs sit next to sounds most people would never guess came from a guitar. The band’s albums Rage Against the Machine and Evil Empire made him one of the most talked-about guitarists of the 1990s.

Morello later played in Audioslave with Chris Cornell, adapting his sound to more melodic hard rock. He has inspired many players to treat pedals and switches as part of the instrument. Rage Against the Machine were inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2023.

What Makes a Guitarist Great?

Ranking guitarists always starts arguments, because greatness on the guitar can mean very different things. Speed and technique are easy to notice, but they are only part of the story.

Feel and Phrasing

A single bent note with the right vibrato can say more than a fast scale. B.B. King and David Gilmour are proof that the notes you leave out matter as much as the ones you play.

A Sound All Their Own

The greatest players can be recognized in a few notes. That can come from technique, like Wes Montgomery’s thumb, or from gear, like Brian May’s homemade Red Special.

Influence on Other Players

Many players on this list are here because they changed what came after them. Chuck Berry, Robert Johnson and Eddie Van Halen each started styles that thousands of guitarists copied.

How to Listen to a Great Guitarist

Next time you play songs by the guitarists on this list, try listening for more than the solo.

Five Things to Listen For

  1. Rhythm: listen to how the guitar locks in with the drums and bass, like Keith Richards on “Honky Tonk Women.”
  2. Tone: notice whether the sound is warm and round or sharp and biting.
  3. Space: pay attention to the gaps between notes, not just the notes themselves.
  4. Dynamics: listen for how a player builds from soft to loud within a song.
  5. Serving the song: notice when the guitar steps back to make room for the vocals.

Start With the Classics

A great place to start is with landmark albums like Electric Ladyland, Live at the Regal, Led Zeppelin IV and Van Halen. Each one shows a different idea of what a great guitarist can be.

title: The Pop World Reacts to the Loss of Dolly Parton
content:
In a time when people can’t seem to agree on anything, they could agree on Dolly. She was a beacon for harmony and warrior for equality. Through her songs, but more importantly through her actions, Dolly Parton was the ultimate activist for unanimity. Her musical legacy is unrivaled, but her true legacy is that of caring and empathy. Sadly, Parton passed away in August of 2026. She was 80 years old.   

Dolly didn’t leave anyone behind or cut anyone out. As American journalist Shima Oliaee states, “Her radical acceptance of all kinds of people…in recent years earned her the nickname of the ‘Great Unifier.’” A moniker well deserved. She was also the definitive pop star. It seems the only prerequisite for Dolly’s demographic is decent folks with a fondness for good music. Thus, Parton is one of only a select few that are members of both the Country Music and the Rock & Roll Halls of Fame. Indeed, her passing is felt across the full music spectrum as well as the entire entertainment community. These are only a few reactions from the pop world concerning the Loss of Dolly Parton.   

Reese Witherspoon: I count my lucky stars that I called Dolly my friend… Throughout my entire career, she sent me little notes of encouragement and support, telling me to be the light in people’s lives and listen to my angels. Always signed: “I will always love you. Dolly, I miss you already. Your talent, your wisdom and your beautiful spirit lit up our lives. Go soar with your angels…. We will always love you.”

Grand Ole Opry: “There is no doubt Dolly’s mark on the world, and on us here at the Grand Ole Opry, will be deeply felt for generations. She taught us to always lead with kindness, generosity, and compassion.” Dolly first performed at the Opry in 1959 at the age of 13.

Beyoncé: “You were the barometer. The North Star. Bold and brilliant. Talented and tenacious. You taught so many lessons on how to be uniquely oneself. I am grateful for your art, your heart, your generosity, your humor, your entrepreneurship. I’m honored that I had the privilege to work with you. You are truly one of one. Rest peacefully.”

Colman Domingo: “Dolly taught us that you can be anything and do anything and to do it with kindness. What a light. We are all grateful that we lived in a time of Dolly Parton. We will always love her.”

Sabrina Carpenter: “An angel walking the earth. I will cherish our laughter and conversations. I will keep your wisdom, your playful outlook on life, and perfect sense of humor in my pocket for the rainy days. There will never be another you and how lucky are we all to have experienced your singular magic as well as your once in a lifetime voice, songs, and heart.” 

Paul McCartney: “She was so bubbly and full of life it is difficult to take in the news that she has passed. Her songwriting, her singing and her philanthropy were unrivaled in the world of country music. It is hard to imagine living in a world without Dolly. She was a very clever business woman who understood the value of her music and, most importantly, the effect that she had on the people of the world. I am so proud to have known her and admire her unique talents. Thanks Dolly for the beautiful music you gave me and the whole world…You were the best.”  

Peyton Manning: “There was only one Dolly and I feel lucky to have known her. We’ll miss you, Dolly. Tennessee won’t be the same without her!”

Oprah Winfrey: “This girl from the Smoky Mountains of Tennessee dreamed a life and then lived a life bigger than she could have ever imagined. Giving so generously to others in ways we saw and ways we didn’t. No one like her. She brought the light, and we are all better because she was here. God bless you, Dolly—you earned your wings.”

Jamie Lee Curtis: “They say don’t meet your heroes. They were wrong about her.”

Taylor Swift: “A world without Dolly doesn’t feel possible, real, or right. But because of the eternally generous way she spent her time on this earth and the countless lives she changed for the better, her legacy will be an everlasting one…Somehow, she was true grace and true grit, all in one dazzling person.”

Mick Jagger: “What a wonderful songwriter and singer Dolly was. She brought so many people together, we will all miss her so much.”

Miley Cyrus: “The feeling of losing my Aunt Dolly is beyond what feels right to share. Our most sacred moments were private, and they’ll stay there behind the stage, beneath the glamour & between our hearts…Me and Dolly, we are eternal. Nothing in this life could ever tear us apart and I’m going to see her again. And I can’t fucking wait cause I miss her.”

title: Grand Theft Auto VI: The Festival Brings Vice City’s Soundtrack to Life in Miami
content:
The wait for Grand Theft Auto VI has been long, but Rockstar Games is making the launch feel like an event. On November 21, two days after the game hits shelves, the publisher will turn Mana Wynwood in Miami into a slice of Leonida for Grand Theft Auto VI: The Festival. Expect two stages and a stacked lineup, plus a crowd that came for the music as much as the game.

A Lineup That Sounds like a GTA Radio Station

The roster reads like someone scrolled through the in-game dial and picked the best of every genre. Cactus Jack presents Travis Scott headlines, with Don Toliver, Kodak Black, and Sofaygo rounding out the rap side of the bill. That run covers trap and melodic rap alongside Florida’s underground.

Cardi B brings the Bronx to Miami, and Metro Boomin handles the production-heavy end of the bill. Justice will perform a DJ set, a fitting choice since the duo composed the game’s original score. The lineup also reaches into Latin and global sounds with Rauw & Friends, Tainy, and Ca7riel & Paco Amoroso, plus back-to-back sets from Nick León B2B DJ Python and Prospa B2B Skream. The Dare B2B Fcukers close out the second stage.

Tickets Are Not a Simple Purchase

If you want to go, you can’t just buy a ticket. Rockstar is using a pre-sale lottery system operated through DICE, with codes distributed by Laylo. The lottery closes on Tuesday, November 10 at 4:00 p.m. ET. Winners are drawn at 7:00 p.m. ET that same day, and tickets go on sale for those winners on Wednesday, November 11 at 12:00 p.m. ET.

There are a few rules worth knowing. You must be 17 or older to attend, and you’ll need a valid photo ID.

Tickets are limited to two per purchaser and are non-transferable. Rockstar also warns that you should create your DICE account immediately after entering the lottery, using the same email and phone number, or you risk being flagged as a bot and removed from the draw.

The Venue and the Vibe

Mana Wynwood sits at 318 NW 23rd St, Miami, and all ticketholders will enter through 5th Avenue. There is no parking on-site, so plan on rideshare. The venue is familiar to anyone who has attended III Points, and it’s a fitting backdrop for a festival that treats a game launch like a night out.

For one night, Miami will feel a little more like Vice City. The music will be loud and the stages packed. Somewhere in the crowd, someone will be counting down the hours until they can finally play GTA VI. The festival celebrates the game’s soundtrack and the city that inspired it. If you’re lucky enough to win the lottery, you’ll be part of a launch event that feels like a party Rockstar wanted to throw.

title: Feelings: Junior Jack, Mark Knight and James Hurr Rework a Classic
content:
Junior Jack‘s “My Feeling” came out in 1999 and has been a staple for house heads around the globe ever since. Now Vito Lucente has brought Mark Knight and James Hurr in to reshape it for a new run. The result is called “Feelings,” and it keeps the character of the original while adding a harder low end and a sharper mix.

The new version could have been a simple remaster but Knight and Hurr went further. They built “Feelings” around the original’s vocal and groove, then tightened the low end and sharpened the mix. The result sounds bigger than the 1999 release without losing what made it work. That balance is harder to hit than it sounds. Rework a classic too carefully and you end up with a museum piece. Push it too far and you lose the reason people loved it in the first place. Knight and Hurr seem to understand that. They did not try to fix something that was not broken. They just made it hit harder.

“Feelings” is out now on Toolroom Records. Some hooks do not age and a good rework does not need to reinvent the wheel. Sometimes all a record needs is a fresh set of ears and a tighter mix. That is what this version delivers.

title: Ranking All the Paramore Albums
content:
In 2005, Paramore released their debut album, All We Know Is Falling. It wasn’t necessarily the greatest debut the world has ever seen, but it did at least have potential. Over the course of their subsequent albums, Paramore realized that potential and then some. Now over 15 years into their recording career, they’ve come a long, long way from their inauspicious start, winning Grammy awards, Top Ten hits, and critical acclaim. Here’s how we rank all the Paramore albums from worst to best.

6. All We Know Is Falling

Some bands never manage to top their first album. Paramore isn’t that kind of band. All We Know Is Falling isn’t offensive, but as soundbitereviews.com notes, there’s plenty of reminders of just how young and inexperienced the band were at the time of its release. Songs like All We Know, My Heart, and Emergency show an immense amount of potential, but others (Never Let This Go and Whoa, in particular) sound like they were written by kids, for kids.

Considering lead singer Hayley Williams was only sixteen and drummer Zac Farro was only fourteen at the time, the immaturity is entirely understandable – if not completely listenable. To add to the album’s woes, bassist Jeremy Davis left (for the first but not the last time) in the middle of making the album – having a band member up and leave during recording rarely spells good things for an album, and it certainly doesn’t here. Yet for all its issues, the gritty, emo-inflected style and sheer enthusiasm of the band make it hard to write the album off completely.

It may pale in comparison to their later efforts, but every band needs to start somewhere, and some have started at much worse places than this. Released on July 26, 2005, the album failed to make it onto the Billboard 200 but did manage to reach No. 30 on Billboard’s Heatseekers Chart. It enjoyed a better reception in the UK, peaking at No. 51 on the Albums Chart and No.4 on the Rock Chart.

5. The Final Riot!

As returnofrock.com notes, it’s rare for a band to sound better live than on a studio recording, but on The Final Riot! Paramore comes close. Recorded at the Congress Theater in Chicago during The Final Riot! Summer Tour, it showcases some spectacular vocals from Hayley Williams and an incredibly tight performance from the rest of the band. The song list is excellent, featuring a good helping of the choicest cuts from Riot!. Released on November 25, 2008, it peaked at No. 22 on the US Billboard Rock Albums chart and No. 18 on the UK Rock Chart.

4. Riot!

If there’s one good thing about a disappointing debut, it’s that the pressure is off for its follow-up. Fortunately, Riot! was a major step forward for the band, who sound altogether tighter, more focussed, and more mature than they do on its predecessor. Musically, it’s more adventurous: the sound they’d cultivated on All We Know Is Falling is still there, but there’s enough diversity to give it crossover potential, with some critics comparing its pop-rock sensibilities to those of Kelly Clarkson and Avril Lavigne.

Not everyone loved it (Gareth Dobson at Drowned in Sound was one of the most scathing critics, calling it “one long, sugar-infused bleat”) but plenty did, with Stylus Magazine describing it as “irrepressible power pop” and naming it to their 50 albums of 2007 list. Ultimately, it isn’t an album that’s going to be remembered by many as the band’s best. However, the huge advance it made on their debut showed that Paramore were a band that could grow and improve, something they’ve continued to do on almost each subsequent release. Released on June 12, 2007, it peaked at No. 15 on the Billboard 200 and has since achieved triple platinum status in the US.

3. Paramore

As What Culture says, after the departure of the Farro brothers in 2010, Paramore’s future was cast into doubt. When Hayley Williams started making multiple guest appearances on other artists’ albums, a lot of fans thought the band’s days were over. But then, in 2013, they made a defiant return with Paramore. Artistically, they’d never sounded more adventurous, dabbling with everything from bubblegum pop to new wave and funk. When the experiments hit their mark (as they do on tracks like Fast In My Car, Anklebiters, Proof, and Future), they work brilliantly.

The problem is, at 17 tracks long, the ideas run out before the album does. There’s plenty of thrills, but far too much filler in between. With more judicious editing, it could easily have ranked as one of their most accomplished efforts. As it is, it falls just a little short. For all that, it became the band’s most successful album till that point, earning them a No. 1 on the US Billboard 200 and topping the charts in the UK, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand, Brazil, Argentina, and Mexico. It also earned them their first Grammy for the single Ain’t It Fun.

2. After Laughter

After a four-year hiatus, Paramore returned in 2017 with After Laughter. Sonically, it’s a world away from their punky roots, with the band diving headfirst into the synth-pop sounds and new wave vibes they’d begun embracing on 2013’s Paramore. Although the change in direction may have left some fans longing for the emo sounds of their earlier days, most listeners welcomed the shift, especially on highlights such as Hard Times, Fake Happy, and Grudges. All in all, it’s a remarkably focused, cohesive album that fully deserved the warm reception it received on its release. Released on May 12, 2017, it became their third Top Ten album in the US, charting at No. 6 on the Billboard 200.

1. Brand New Eyes

By 2008, Paramore were in trouble. A year of nonstop touring had left them experiencing “internal issues,” canceling shows, and struggling to come up with new material. The problems led to speculation that Riot! would prove to be the band’s swansong. But then, in 2009, they released Brand New Eyes, an album that silenced their critics for good and proved once and for all that a little tension never does a band any harm. Hailed as their most mature project to date, the album was a smash hit, winning a slew of accolades (including a Grammy nomination for the single The Only Exception and a Kerrang! Award for Best Album) and charting at No. 2 on the Billboard 200 – their highest charting position until 2013’s Paramore. It also topped the charts in the UK, Ireland, Australia, and New Zealand.

title: One Uber, One Demo: The Story Behind Audien and Luke Alexander’s ‘7 Miles High’
content:
It’s morning in Chicago. Luke Alexander sits in the back of an Uber headed to the airport. The sky is still that flat, early gray, and the city slides past the window in a blur of wet pavement and half-lit storefronts. Luke hasn’t really slept. He’s coming off a festival, his ears still ringing a little, his bag wedged between his feet.

On his phone is a track he’s only been working on for a quick second. He thinks it might be something, but he wants another set of ears on it, and there’s no studio anywhere in reach. This Uber is the closest thing to one he’s had all weekend.

So he plays what he has. The demo comes through the car’s speakers. It’s rough around the edges, a sketch more than a song, but it fills the car anyway as the Uber merges onto the expressway. Luke turns to the guy next to him and asks what he thinks.

That guy is Nate Rathbun. Most people know him as Audien.

That Uber ride became “7 Miles High.” Out now via Enhanced, the single pairs the melodic instincts behind Audien’s GRAMMY-nominated career and his Progressive House Never Died (PHND) movement with the grittier, groove-first house Alexander built in New York nightlife. For Audien, it’s a lean into house. For Alexander, it’s his first collaboration at this level after cutting his teeth in the city’s countless clubs.

We caught up with both artists as the first-day numbers were rolling in. They walked us through the demo’s evolution, New York’s mood swings, and why genre debates belong on ancestry.com.

Zac: How did you two initially cross paths and decide to work together on “7 Miles High”? Was there something specific about each other’s style that you felt would complement your own approach to making music?

Audien: Luke and I had talked about working on something together when the right idea came along, and luckily it landed for us super naturally in an Uber. I’ve always liked the energy and edge he brings to his music, and I thought combining that with my more melodic approach could lead somewhere interesting.

Luke: Funny story… We were on our way to the airport in an Uber after both playing a festival in Chicago. I was listening on the speakers in the Uber to this track that I had been working on for a quick second. The car was the closest thing to a studio I had that weekend. I asked Nate what he thought, and he gave great input, so I asked if he wanted to work on it with me and make it a collab. Nate brought the record to life after that. We went back and forth and landed where it is now, and I couldn’t be happier.

Zac: What did the earliest versions of “7 Miles High” sound like, and was there an immediate feeling that the track had found its identity, or was that something that had to develop a bit more over time?

Audien: When Luke first played the track for me, we knew it had lots of potential. We kept refining it until the production felt big and euphoric while still having his signature house sound driving it.

Luke: The earliest versions were pretty tame. By the time I got it to the version I shared with Nate, it had a lot more energy and legs to it. The goal was to make something modern that pushed the boundaries of what’s being done in dance-pop, while pulling from tech house, indie dance, and progressive house to create a real blend of both of our sounds. I think we did that pretty well, if I’m being honest.

Zac: How did each of you contribute to the production, and do you get the sense that there was a distinct element or creative decision that significantly shaped the direction of the record?

Audien: I think our different approaches are really what shaped the record. Luke brings a grittier edge to his production, and I naturally gravitate toward melody and emotion, so “7 Miles High” became a really nice meeting point between those two worlds.

Luke: I started out in the industry as a progressive house DJ, and as a fan of Nate’s music, so I trusted that his melodic, emotional sound would complement the techier side of what I do. I also wanted to give him the freedom to really influence the record and push it further into that melodic space.

Zac: Luke, the finished track has a definitive house feel. Was there ever some consideration to take a more progressive house approach that leans more toward the grand, emotional sound Audien is known for?

Luke: I’ve been a fan of progressive house since I was a kid, and I think this record pays homage to that sound in a really nice way without ever feeling predictable. To me, it meshes both worlds together really well. At the end of the day, genres don’t mean that much to me. The whole battle of what’s cool, what genre something belongs to, or which genre is somehow superior is corny. Make dope shit. Make people happy. Make people escape. Make people dance. If the record does all of that, who cares what you call it? Send it to ancestry.com and let them figure it out.

Zac: Audien, the uniquely euphoric sound of progressive house has become a massive part of your identity as an artist. How do you maintain that connection to the genre while exploring new styles?

Audien: Progressive house will always be a huge part of who I am as an artist. It’s the sound I fell in love with, and PHND has given me this incredible platform to keep celebrating it, but I also never want to feel limited to making one type of music. For me, it’s about keeping that emotion and energy at the core of what I do while giving myself the freedom to explore different sounds.

Zac: Luke, New York is a one-of-a-kind city with culture and flair like nowhere else in the world. How did your background in the city influence your approach to “7 Miles High”?

Luke: New York is fucking moody, dude. Some days you wake up and the city is gritty as shit and you feel like a gangster. Other days it’s aggressive, other days it’s artsy and futuristic, and then sometimes it feels like you’re living in a fucking rom-com. Sometimes it’s sad. The seasons completely change the emotion of the city, too. I think the record does the same thing. On the surface, it’s a happy song, but there’s this underlying moodiness to it that carries a lot more emotion. It really depends on where you’re at when you listen to it. It can feel freeing, it can feel healing, it can feel nostalgic, or it can feel sad. And then another day you put it on and it just makes you happy. I think New York has always had that same emotional ambiguity for me.

Zac: The track has some real energy and bounce. Can you elaborate on a few of the emotions you wanted to capture or experiences that were on your mind when creating “7 Miles High”?

Luke: It’s got the groove I’ve been pushing in my records, but there’s also a lot of that blog-house influence from the indie world of the 2010s and even before that. Then you have the vocal, which again plays such a huge role in defining the record. Those three things together are really the DNA of the song.

Zac: Audien, you’ve been expanding the PHND world this year, including three shows in New York in less than 30 hours this summer. First, what was that weekend like, and how do you feel that a track like “7 Miles High” fits into that bigger picture for you?

Audien: New York was a really special weekend. Getting to play three completely different shows in less than 30 hours and see the PHND community show up throughout the weekend was incredible. “7 Miles High” is definitely more house-driven than what people might traditionally associate with PHND, but that’s part of the bigger picture for me. PHND lets me continue championing progressive house while my own music can keep evolving and exploring new sounds.

Zac: Luke, what has this collaboration meant to you, and does it change or expand on what you plan to explore through your music next?

Luke: It’s definitely a milestone for me. It’s my first collaboration at this level, but what makes it more meaningful is that it happened with someone I consider family. There’s already a lot of overlap between our worlds. We share a manager and an agent, and there’s a real relationship between us, so it all feels pretty natural. But this wasn’t some coordinated play date where everyone said, “You guys have the same team, go make a record.” It was purely the right record, the right people, at the right time. Had I missed my flight that morning (which I almost did), I would not have been at our show and would not have been able to show Nate the demo. That’s how I want collaborations to happen.

As far as what comes next, I think it just reinforces the direction I’ve already been moving in. I want to keep making records that can live in different worlds without being overly concerned with where they’re supposed to fit. And I mean, I’m watching the numbers come in from the first 24 hours, and I’ve never had a record move this quickly out of the gate, so clearly we did something right.

Zac: After releasing “7 Miles High,” is there potential for another collaboration between the two of you sometime soon, or is the plan to let fans enjoy this one for a little while before deciding what’s next?

Audien: Never say never. I think we’re both really happy with how this one turned out, and we enjoyed working on the song together.

Luke: Yeah, next time we’re gonna have to go on a bender for three days and see what comes out of it.

Had Alexander missed his flight that morning, there’s no show, no Uber, and no “7 Miles High.” As for a follow-up, Audien is keeping his options open.

Alexander already has a plan: three days, no sleep, and whatever comes out the other side.

title: Supernova’s “When I Close My Eyes” bridges classic, progressive, and modern house
content:
Supernova‘s “When I Close My Eyes” draws from three house traditions: the precision of contemporary tech house, the stripped-back warmth of old-school house, and the rhythmic generosity of disco house. No single influence dominates.

The rhythm lays the foundation. A steady four-to-the-floor pulse provides the anchor, but the percussion work prevents the groove from settling into predictability. Hi-hats and auxiliary drum elements create forward momentum, and the bass sits low and purposeful beneath the surface. The bass does its work without calling attention to itself. The hi-hats and auxiliary drums are where the motion lives, and they keep the track from feeling like a loop.

A track built on repetition needs small variations to stay alive, and “When I Close My Eyes” finds those variations without drawing attention to them. The groove feels steady without feeling static.

The synth and textural work operates somewhere between restraint and engagement. Supernova favor warmer electronic textures over the more aggressive timbres associated with harder tech house, and those warmer sounds recall earlier house traditions. They provide melodic interest without overwhelming the rhythm, which allows the track to breathe. The synths are present and melodic, but they never try to steal the spotlight from the rhythm. That is a mark of confidence in the arrangement. The relationship between synth lines and percussion feels considered. Each element gets sufficient space to register independently, and nothing crowds the mix. “When I Close My Eyes” finds a middle path where every element has room to move.

“When I Close My Eyes” is a well-crafted house release that respects its lineage while maintaining its own identity. We recommend it to listeners seeking intelligent, groove-oriented electronic music.

Supernova – “When I Close My Eyes” is out now on Insomniac’s Factory 93.

title: San Mateo Drive Builds a Slow Burn on “Forever Calling”
content:
San Mateo Drive, the melodic house project of American producer Mateo Gonzalez, presents “Forever Calling.” It landed on the Colorize 2026 Autumn Sampler through Enhanced‘s Colorize imprint.

The rhythmic foundation of “Forever Calling” is a steady four-to-the-floor pulse, the sort of unshakable kick that has anchored house music for decades. But what makes the track interesting is everything that happens around that kick. The percussion does not pile on. It works in measured increments. New textures appear at intervals that feel judged rather than automatic. A shaker enters. A hi-hat shifts slightly in tone. A low-end element gains just enough presence to change the temperature of the room.

This is arrangement as a form of restraint. San Mateo Drive seems to understand that momentum is not the same thing as noise. The track builds, but it builds the way a tide comes in rather than the way a wave crashes. By the time the later sections arrive, the sense of movement feels earned. Nothing has been forced. The energy has been allowed to gather.

“Forever Calling” works in the long middle of a set, when the room has settled into a rhythm and the DJ wants to take the floor somewhere more emotionally complex without losing the groove. The elements get enough room to make their case without overstaying the welcome.

Listeners who want immediate gratification, who want the hook in the first eight bars, will find “Forever Calling” slow. But for those who still believe that progressive house can be progressive in the literal sense, that a track can develop and change and surprise without shouting, this is a strong piece of work.

title: Reload, Rewired: How swedm® Reworked Sebastian Ingrosso and Tommy Trash
content:
Sebastian Ingrosso and Tommy Trash‘s “Reload” landed in September 2012 on Ingrosso‘s Refune label, a muscular progressive house cut built for main stages. A year later, John Martin’s vocals arrived and turned it into something else entirely. That version became a singalong monster, the kind of record that could close a festival set and leave thousands of people hoarse. It is a track with serious baggage, the good kind, loaded with memories of a very specific era in dance music.

So when a remix of “Reload” surfaces in 2026, matching the original is no longer the relevant test. That ship has sailed. What matters is what a new generation hears in it. The answer, at least according to the swedm® collective, is something stranger and more interesting than a straightforward festival refresh.

The Collective Behind the Rework

swedm® is a fluid collective that formed in 2024, a rotating cast of artists with roots in experimental electronic music and the harder edges of club culture. The lineup reads like a crossover fever dream. Varg², jamesjamesjames, Eurohead, Whitearmor, and Skrillex have all been associated with the project, alongside Drain Gang figures like Bladee and Thaiboy Digital. Their stated mission is deceptively simple: keep the Swedish EDM legacy alive while pushing it through a modern, often weird, filter.

That mission makes them the perfect candidates to tackle “Reload.” Pitchfork described swedm®’s work as an attempt to “reappraise the richly earnest sounds of 2010s Swedish EDM,” the kind of pointillistic, high-octave melodies that gave big-room tracks a rush of blood to the head. This is a collective that grew up with this music and understands its emotional pull. They also know how to pull it apart.

The Vibes: A Memory Remixed in Real Time

The swedm® remix of “Reload” does not sound like a 2013 festival bootleg. It runs five minutes and sits around 137 BPM, carrying a different kind of confidence. The familiar melodic bones of the original are there, but they are refracted through a lens that owes as much to trance and ambient textures as it does to progressive house. The result is a track that feels both enormous and oddly intimate, like remembering a packed arena from the quiet of a bedroom years later. There are moments where the track seems to dissolve entirely, only to reassemble itself around a familiar phrase. The effect is hypnotic.

There is a melancholy in it. The synths shimmer and dissolve where the original’s would soar. The drop breathes instead of hitting. For anyone who spent their formative club years in the 2010s, the effect is disarming. You hear a memory being remixed in real time.

For listeners who know the original by heart, the remix offers a strange gift. It lets you hear a familiar song as if for the first time. The notes are the same. The light is different. For younger listeners, it is an entry point, a doorway into a sound that shaped a generation of producers now circling back to it with new tools and new questions. swedm® want to know what 2012 feels like from 2026. Recreating the original is beside the point.

The track is set for release on 6 November 2026 through Refune, the same label that launched the original all those years ago. That circularity feels deliberate. A festival anthem from the early 2010s, remixed by a collective formed to preserve and mutate that very legacy, arriving back on the same imprint. It is a neat story, but the music does not rely on the narrative. The remix stands on its own as a thoughtful, emotionally complex piece of electronic music. It honours the past without being trapped by it. That is a harder trick than it sounds.

title: After Over a Decade, Polar Inc. Releases Debut Album ‘Tragicomedy’
content:
Polar Inc. has finally dropped his debut album, Tragicomedy. The Cape Town producer, real name Adam Spence, has been putting out music for more than ten years and has over 120 million streams, but this is his first full album. Across ten tracks he goes back and forth between everything he’s known for, or as he puts it, “happiness and melancholy, cinematic and clubby, emotion and rhythm.”

A handful of singles came out ahead of the album, including “Sympathy” with Anna-Sophia Henry, “Cerulean,” “For You” featuring Nathan Ball and “Slopes” with Hannah Ray. There’s lore behind the last one — he first started “Slopes” while on tour in San Francisco, and named it after the hills he’d been walking around that day. The rest of the album includes “Holding Me Up” with sadHAPPY, “Le Concorde,” “Apricity,” “Catching Fire” featuring ALLKNIGHT, “Agulhas” and the album’s incredible opener “Prima” – a track that started as a chord progression he kept coming back to while making the album until finally finishing it last.

It took Adam Spence more than a decade to make a full-length record, and Tragicomedy sounds like he used every minute of it.

title: Morgin Madison Plants the Seeds of a New Chapter on Third Album ‘Another Eden
content:
Morgin Madison is starting fresh with his third album, Another Eden, out on Enhanced Recordings. After five singles, the full project is finally here, and it comes from a big turning point for him. Madison got sober in 2025, deleted his social media apps and spent seven months figuring out what music meant to him without the touring, clubs and drinking that used to come with it. “Another Eden is an audio diary of the last year and a half of my life,” Madison says. “I wasn’t sure if I could still make music like I used to, or if I even wanted to.” The whole concept started with a friend telling him his “garden of life” was poisoned and it was up to him to bring it back to life.

Turns out he could still make music, just a little differently. Another Eden steps outside the progressive and melodic sound Madison is known for and bounces between different electronic styles, with each track built around whatever he was feeling at the time. The singles included “The Otherside” with LeyeT, “Healing” with Kindrid and Linney, “Thinking Of U” with HILYTE and Division One, “Follow You” with HILYTE, and “Around You” with Treetalk. “Healing” brings Madison back together with former mau5trap labelmate Kindrid and digs into the anger and uncertainty of that time, while other tracks lean more hopeful. From frustration to optimism, the album covers a lot of ground, and by the end, Madison’s garden looks like it’s growing back just fine.

title: ILLENIUM, Steve Aoki, Galantis, and More Lead Ubbi Dubbi 2027 ‘Canditopia’
content:
Ubbi and Dubbi are leaving Earth behind. Disco Presents has unveiled the lineup and theme for Ubbi Dubbi 2027, and the Texas festival’s two mascots are taking fans to Canditopia, a candy planet where house grooves and bass drops share the same skyline.

title: The all-new XS was rebuilt around the booth
content:
XS is officially back. And better than ever.

And now that the room is finally visible, it’s clear Wynn didn’t just repaint.

The official design language is “retro-futurist opulence”: reflective brass, bronze, and chrome, saturated color, sculptural forms, and surfaces that glow. A moving ceiling hangs over the floor. The centerpiece is the DJ booth. It’s finished in mirrored gold and designed for both DJs and live acts, and Wynn built the subwoofers and center-fill speakers into the structure itself so the system is felt rather than seen.

title: Martron Teams Up With Tauklo on “Hit The Road,” the First Taste of His Forthcoming Drive EP
content:
Martron has been on a run this year, and he isn’t slowing down. The Los Angeles-based producer, multi-instrumentalist, and classically trained musician has linked up with longtime collaborator Tauklo for “Hit The Road,” a bright indie-electronic single that serves as the first look at his upcoming Drive EP.

“Hit The Road” is built around a bouncy drum & bass groove, melodies that stick with you after the first listen, and Tauklo’s unmistakable vocal delivery. The track is about taking risks and pushing forward no matter what gets in the way. Its refrain turns into a mantra: when something is motivating you to move, you go before the moment passes. Martron closes it out with a burst of flute chords, an organic touch that stands out against the colorful electronic production around it.

The song started as an old idea that Martron kept coming back to over the past couple of years. He knew it had the makings of the lead single for Drive, but it needed the right voice.

“‘Hit The Road’ came together out of nowhere and pretty fast from an old idea I started a couple years ago. I worked on it every now and again and loved how infectious the melodies are and wanted this to be the single for Drive, but I wanted the right vocalist for it. That’s when I reached out to Tauklo, who I’ve worked with for a little over a decade and consider a brother,” Martron said. “I’ve produced a bunch of records for him over the years, but this is our second collaboration by name that we’ve put out together and a very special one for sure.”

The single lands just months after Martron released his EP Passion in March. That record was focused on self-discovery, digging into identity, roots, and what ultimately defines a person. Drive picks up where that introspection left off and asks what comes next. What motivates you? What pushes you to get better? What are you actually capable of? Martron made the EP in just three months, and he’s leaning into a more energetic, heavier, and darker side of his sound to answer those questions.

It has been a big year for Martron outside of the studio too. He has picked up attention from UKF, Roland, and GQ, and he was featured in Apple’s “Shot on iPhone” campaign. His music has also earned support from ODESZA, NGHTMRE, SLANDER, Niiko x SWAE, and Steve Aoki, along with placements on Spotify playlists like Bass Arcade, Chill Tracks, and Metropolis. If “Hit The Road” is any indication of where Drive is headed, the rest of the EP should be a lot of fun.

Martron and Tauklo’s “Hit The Road” is out now. The Drive EP arrives Tuesday, October 27. Stream “Hit The Road” here.

title: WORSHIP: The Brotherhood Taking Drum & Bass Worldwide
content:
WORSHIP, the collaborative project uniting Sub Focus, Dimension, Culture Shock, and 1991, is bringing drum and bass to new audiences across the globe. After years of establishing themselves as solo artists, the four British DJs have joined forces to showcase the genre’s versatility through collaborative productions, dynamic live sets, and an unmistakable shared energy.

As the group continues its North American arena tour, I caught up with WORSHIP at their sold-out Brooklyn Storehouse tour stop, to discuss their early introductions to drum and bass, the creative process behind their collaborative sound, and their ambitions for the future of the genre.

LIANA: How did each of you first discover drum and bass, and what initially pulled you into the genre?

SUB FOCUS: In school during break time, my friend put on a compilation of jungle music, which was the genre that came before drum and bass. There was a song called “Incredible,” which was a big hit in 1994. It was the craziest style of music I had ever heard. I had never heard anything like it, and I was obsessed from that point onward.

CULTURE SHOCK: In between the mainstream radio stations, you would tune through the FM dial, and there would be these illegal pirate stations broadcasting jungle. I didn’t even know what the name was back then, but it was these crazy sounds of chopped-up, sped-up drum beats. 

SUB FOCUS: That was one of the things that made it so exciting early on. It was extremely underground, and it took a while for it to filter into the mainstream.

Now, in the UK, drum and bass has become a really popular genre, with a few select songs even reaching number one in the charts. It’s been an exciting journey to watch it grow, and I think our ambition is to expose more people to it, show them the type of drum and bass we’re into, and represent it in the best way we can.

LIANA: What does it feel like to be at the forefront of pushing the genre into North America? Are there any other regions you hope to expand into, and where do you see drum and bass going next?

DIMENSION: It feels amazing and like a massive privilege to be pushing the genre here in North America. Obviously, with that comes an element of responsibility. There’s a huge amount of culture deeply rooted here, and we want to honor and respect that while also making it accessible and open to new people, because I think that’s a really positive thing.

We set out to try and conquer America five or six years ago, and it’s been an amazing journey. We’re starting to do some really big shows, and this is our first-ever arena tour, which we never really thought would be possible.

The next territory we’ve really got our eyes on is Asia. We’ve been playing there, and we’re doing our first-ever show in China in a couple of weeks. For me, it’s an amazing territory with so much potential. That’s the next place on the horizon, so it’s exciting.

SUB FOCUS: It’s also worth mentioning that we just went to South America for the first time and played in Medellín at EDC. That’s another really exciting area. Dimension is actually half Spanish, and we’re working on some Spanish-language music as well. We really want to take drum and bass worldwide and bring it to some new places.

LIANA: Can you describe your creative process as a group? Since you all have individual touring schedules, how do you find time to make new music together?

CULTURE SHOCK: Laptops and planes! Because you’re constantly touring, it’s just little, short windows or where you’re in a hotel for a bit.

DIMENSION: One thing that really separates us from other groups is that we’ve all had our own individual and successful solo careers. We’re all masters of our craft, so when you put that together, we’re stronger than the sum of our parts. In a band, someone might play the drums or do one particular thing, but we’ve all done it ourselves, which makes us a lot stronger. That’s why I think it’s worked so well.

SUB FOCUS: We’re all-rounders because we’ve done this individually as solo artists, but we’ve got studios in London and link up as much as possible. This year, we’ve been doing a lot of sessions together, and have been linking up to write a lot of tracks.

CULTURE SHOCK: It’s fun being in a studio together because we’re used to operating on our own, maybe with a singer or songwriter. When there’s four of us together, we can joke around a lot, and when the vibe is really good and there’s a good idea, it gets very exciting quite quickly. You can make something really fast because everybody’s making different parts of the songs.

And if you’re not fast enough, your idea gets vetoed!

LIANA: What does each of you bring individually to WORSHIP? Where do your strengths and creative approaches differ?

SUB FOCUS: I think our skill sets are similar, but they overlap a lot. Culture Shock is amazing at making sounds. I tend to look at songs from a more zoomed-out perspective, and I think I’m more into finishing things. 1991 is amazing at starting things and remixing things. Dimension’s stuff tends to be quite song-oriented. We all have our own strengths and different areas of specialization.

LIANA: How do you approach building a WORSHIP set? Who decides the tracklist, the order, and the transitions?

SUB FOCUS: There’s so much arguing, and physical fights! (Just kidding).

It depends on the type of set we’re doing. Sometimes we’re very off the cuff, and sometimes we’re more planned. We spend a long time trying to figure out cool transitions and brainstorm together. 

CULTURE SHOCK: I think we have a similar mindset about how sets should flow. There’s a certain energy at the start, a different type of energy in the middle, and then something else at the end. It makes sense that we all play together now because we’re going on that same journey.

SUB FOCUS: We have quite similar musical inspirations. I definitely think about building a set the way a house or techno DJ would, where it’s a journey. Sometimes drum and bass mixing can be very jarring, with crazy double drops and things like that. Our style is to have really nice, smooth transitions and big build-ups. We’re approaching it from more of a house and techno perspective.

LIANA: As the tour continues, what do you hope people take away from seeing WORSHIP perform live?

SUB FOCUS: We hope people really enjoy the shows. We’re trying to showcase the side of drum and bass that we feel represents what it’s all about. We want new people to come to the shows, as well as existing fans, and have an amazing time.

1991: I really like it when you get a message from someone online saying, “That was my first drum and bass show,” and it was a WORSHIP show. If we can convert more people into drum and bass fans, I think that’s a really cool thing.

DIMENSION: The whole point is that it’s really fun. We take it seriously, but at the same time, we’re always having so much fun onstage, and we really want that energy to translate to the crowd. Getting people onstage with us is a big thing, too. We just want to convert as many nonbelievers as we can.

CULTURE SHOCK: Drum and bass has a unique energy because it’s faster than anything else. When it goes off and there’s a big reaction from the crowd, that reaction is like nothing else. There’s nothing that compares to it, so we want to bring that feeling to as many people as possible.

LIANA: Finally, do you have a favorite tour memory or is there a dream venue you’d still love to play?

DIMENSION: We’re quite spoiled in that our dream venues keep getting ticked off. After spending the week in New York, our next dream venue would be Madison Square Garden.

CULTURE SHOCK: We were just outside taking a photo and thinking, “We really need to play here.” That would be cool. It would be crazy.

1991: We’re manifesting it right now.

As WORSHIP continues to take drum and bass to new heights, the four artists remain focused on expanding the genre’s reach while building on the creative chemistry that makes their collaboration unique.

 With their first arena tour marking another milestone in their journey, Sub Focus, Dimension, Culture Shock, and 1991 are proving that drum and bass belong on the world’s biggest stages. And if their Madison Square Garden ambitions are any indication, WORSHIP’s next chapter could be its biggest yet.

title: New Godflesh & Jesu with Phoebe too
content:
The great Jon Wurster (The Mountain Goats, The Bob Mould Band, Superchunk, The Best Show with Tom Scharpling) is a prolific drummer and one of the funniest people on earth. One of my favorite Wursterisms™ is that he utilizes the hashtag #rocknrollweirdness on Instagram when posting images of incongruous moments in rock n’ roll. Whether it’s a picture of The Who holding their Who Are You release party on the Hollywood set of the TV show Battlestar Galactica, Oasis hanging with Wesley Willis, or Motörhead drummer Philthy Animal Taylor and W.A.S.P. guitarist Chris Holmes having ice cream on a nice day, Wurster is a master curator of singular images of #rocknrollweirdness.

It’s rare for an instance of #rocknrollweirdness to land so profoundly with me that it gives me the energy to take finger-to-keyboard for the first time in years. Yet it recently came to my attention that master of heviosity Justin K. Broadrick was recently tapped by mainstream indie icon Phoebe Bridgers to play guitar on two tracks of her August 14, 2026 release Lost Weekend. Justin performs on track #5, “Bobby,” as well as on the ‘hidden’ track “Best Dressed” (track D17 on the vinyl and Track 00 on CD). Broadrick is involved with many different personal projects, each with their own particular signature sonic qualities, so it is important to note that he performs on these tracks under his Jesu moniker. And although I find his contributions to be buried under too many layers of over-production, the Broadrick aficionado can immediately recognize Jesu’s signature guitar sound in the first 15-seconds of “Bobby.” Lost Weekend was the Number 1 album in the UK and debuted at No. 2 on the Billboard 200. This is almost definitely the first time Justin has been that high in the charts.

But there was more! Phoebe Bridgers then released “On Video,” her song from the new A24 film Primetime. You can listen to it below. Oh and guess what? Justin Broadrick played bass and guitar on that song. As you probably know by now, Phoebe is also in the movie, and has been playing the song on tour.

These aren’t the first instances that Justin and Phoebe’s careers have intersected. Back in 2021, again under the Jesu moniker, Justin remixed Phoebe’s Boygenius bandmate Julien Baker’s track “Favor.” Justin not only executed the remix, but he also played guitars on the track which also features Phoebe Bridgers (and Lucy Dacus) on backing vocals. Check that track out below.

In other Justin K. Broadrick news, we’ve had a few months to let it sink in that the mighty Godflesh has retired from touring due to ongoing health issues plaguing Justin. The good news is that prior to his tour-ending surgery, Justin and Benny had an entire new Godflesh album pretty much already in the can. The album, entitled Decay, dropped on September 25 via Relapse Records and is available in all the formats, including vinyl in all kinds of colors and patterns.

Fortunately, all of the recordings for Decay were completed long before the surgery, vocals included… although the back end of a couple of songs were recorded with the hernia itself, and that was a struggle. I was already aware that the GODFLESH shout, so to speak, was exacerbating the hernia greatly, as was every GODFLESH performance in the lead-up to the surgery once the hernia appeared, and the hernia was mostly caused by year upon year of shouting in GODFLESH. The album was mixed post-surgery, and while I was still in some pain and considerable discomfort, but fortunately GODFLESH is generally me expressing my pain, albeit [usually] mental, philosophical and existential, whereas this was physical pain.

You can listen to “Living/Ending” below and do some heavy duty ordering of the vinyl.

I interviewed Justin back in 2014 and would love to interview him again someday to discuss all of his projects BUT Godflesh. Until that happens, both Guitar World and The Guardian have published very good interviews with him that do a great job bringing fans up to speed with the current state of Justin’s world.

Staying on the fest’s Friday hardcore stage for a second: playing before Haywire and the recently-announed, no-longer secret guest Knocked Loose, we want to highlight NY heavy hardcore band Missing Link whose intesity blows us away every time we get the chance to catch them (including sometimes with Haywire). Great live show. Don’t mess up and miss them in Louisville.

Hot Mulligan

Louder than Life also brings the pop punk, and the post-hardcore and emo-leaning Lansing, Michigan band Hot Mulligan are doing it better than most right now. Now four full lengths into their career, the band has become a festival staple, somtimes a rare mosh pit-inducing band on a lineup (like when we saw them at Gov Ball and Lolla), and sometimes right where they belong like in between Alkaline Trio and Jimmy Eat World in Louisville in Thursday. Always a super fun time, we can’t get enough of their energy, their humor, and their infectious hooks.

Danzig

The man, the myth, the legend. Danzig on this year’s fest officially brings it over the top for this Danzig-obsesed writer.
